cards.question: Two encoders emit identical bytes today. Must their decoders be interchangeable forever?
cards.answer: No. Matching a few outputs does not establish the whole protocol contract. Test the complete supported input domain and malformed inputs before claiming interchangeability.

cards.question: Where should a client choose the codec family for one session?
cards.answer: Choose one factory at the session boundary and obtain both products from it. Choosing each product independently makes accidental mixed families easier.

cards.question: Would one encode/decode object be simpler than two product interfaces?

cards.question: Why test all ten digits instead of only seven?
cards.answer: The domain is tiny, so exhaustive valid-input checks are cheap. They catch endpoint and off-by-one defects that a single demonstration misses.

cards.question: Does a unique_ptr<Decoder> express protocol compatibility?

cards.question: What should happen to d=04 in this chapter's protocol?

cards.question: How can a new family be added without editing round_trip?
cards.answer: Implement matching Encoder and Decoder products plus a CodecFactory. round_trip depends on those interfaces and checks that decoding recovers the original digit.

cards.question: Why does build return a Plan value instead of a reference to the draft?

cards.question: Should add reject a draft total above ninety immediately in this implementation?

cards.question: Is resetting a builder the same as destroying a finished Plan?

cards.question: When would a plain Plan constructor be preferable?
cards.answer: When all required values are known together and construction has few choices. A builder helps when a valid result needs several ordered or named steps and drafts may be incomplete.

cards.question: Why can named return PlanBuilder& safely here?

cards.question: What test detects accidental accumulation across reset?
cards.answer: Build an old draft, reset, then build a new seven-minute plan. Assert the new total is seven and the old Plan still has its original total.

cards.question: Why is a director optional rather than another required object?

cards.question: Why is copying a unique_ptr member not a valid deep-copy implementation?
cards.answer: unique_ptr deliberately forbids copying ownership. The copy constructor must allocate a new string and copy the string value, giving each object its own release responsibility.

cards.question: Can clone return the same object under a new unique_ptr?
cards.answer: No. Two independent unique_ptr owners of one address would both delete it. A clone must be a distinct owned object under this contract.

cards.question: Why test destruction of the original before using the clone?
cards.answer: It checks independence of lifetime, not just equality of text. A shallow borrow may appear correct until the original goes away.

cards.question: Would a copied shared_ptr meet the independent-edit contract?
cards.answer: Not by itself. It would share one mutable object, so edits could leak between copies. Immutable sharing or copy-on-write would need an explicitly different design.

cards.question: What does copying through Cue& preserve that slicing Cue by value would lose?
cards.answer: Virtual clone selects the actual concrete kind. Base-value copying would not preserve derived state, and this abstract Cue cannot be instantiated as a value at all.

cards.question: Which part of ListCue makes its default copy sufficient?
cards.answer: vector<string> owns its elements as values. Copying it copies the strings; there are no borrowed element pointers that require a separate deep-copy loop.

cards.question: When is Prototype unnecessary?
cards.answer: When callers know the concrete type and ordinary value copying already expresses the requirement. Prototype helps copy through a common interface without naming every concrete kind.

cards.question: Does safe construction of a local static make every operation thread-safe?
cards.answer: No. C++ protects the one-time initialization. Ticket counter updates still require their own lock, which LocalTickets::take holds across checking and incrementing.

cards.question: Why does the test use LocalTickets instead of resetting the singleton?
cards.answer: A local instance gives each test fresh state without a global reset hook. Resetting a shared service can interfere with other clients and hide order-dependent tests.

cards.question: Does one singleton imply one dispenser across several processes?
cards.answer: No. This object lives within a process. Separate processes have separate memory; a cross-process ticket service needs another coordination mechanism.

cards.question: Why should admit accept TicketSource& rather than fetch the global instance itself?
cards.answer: The dependency becomes visible and replaceable. Production can pass the singleton while tests or independent sessions pass local sources.

cards.question: What is wrong with unlocking between checking the limit and incrementing?
cards.answer: Two threads could both pass the same check before either advances the counter. Keep the state transition within one lock scope.

cards.question: When would a normal owned service be clearer than a singleton?
cards.answer: When lifetime, configuration, or independent sessions matter. One application-owned object passed to clients often gives uniqueness without hidden global access.

cards.question: Why can test execution order expose a hidden singleton dependency?
cards.answer: A prior test may consume tickets. A later test then sees an exhausted global source even though its own local setup is fresh; that is shared state leaking across test boundaries.

cards.question: Why is a reference member not proof that the scale owns its device?
cards.answer: A reference is a borrow. The LegacyScale must outlive ScaleAdapter; destroying the device first leaves the adapter with an invalid reference.

cards.question: Would renaming milligrams to grams be a correct adapter?
cards.answer: No. The units differ by a factor of one thousand. Interface compatibility includes meaning and error behavior, not only method names.

cards.question: Why subtract calibration after conversion in this example?
cards.answer: The offset is measured in grams. Subtracting it from raw milligrams would mix units and produce a numerically plausible but wrong result.

cards.question: When can the adapter be a free function instead of a class?
cards.answer: When the caller needs one conversion and no persistent Scale interface or borrowed device. A class is useful when existing client code already consumes Scale polymorphically.

cards.question: What additional test is needed if floating readings replace integer milligrams?
cards.answer: Test nonfinite values and rounding near boundaries. The current integer device cannot produce NaN, but a new floating device can.

cards.question: Does a valid converted value prove the device reading was valid?
cards.answer: No. A negative device error might become plausible after careless arithmetic. Validate the raw error signal before converting or calibrating.

cards.question: Why keep light_enough independent of LegacyScale?
cards.answer: Its rule is about grams and a Scale contract. Keeping the old device API outside the client makes replacement devices easier to integrate and test.

cards.answer: In report policy, not Csv or Brackets. Writers receive an already chosen label and number and should not decide when a count is high.

cards.answer: Often yes, if the behavior is small and the report does not need a persistent polymorphic interface. Bridge describes the separation, not a requirement to maximize classes.

cards.question: Does sharing a const Writer reference guarantee thread safety?

cards.question: Why is an empty Group valid while a null child is invalid?
cards.answer: An empty group has a well-defined sum of zero. A null entry claims a child position without an object on which minutes or steps can be called.

cards.question: Why does Group own children with unique_ptr rather than borrow them?
cards.answer: The tree controls child lifetime. Removing or destroying an owning group recursively destroys its descendants without requiring callers to track each child separately.

cards.question: What change would sharing one child between two parents require?
cards.answer: A different ownership model and a clear counting rule. Shared ownership might keep the child alive, but it would not decide whether the shared work should be counted once or twice.

cards.question: Why check n against 10000 minus total before adding?
cards.answer: The design rejects an over-budget sum before accepting the new total. Checking only after arbitrary signed addition is unsafe in more general unbounded versions.

cards.question: Could a single struct with a variant replace the virtual Work hierarchy?
cards.answer: Yes. A closed set of node kinds may be clearer as values with a tagged alternative. The interface hierarchy is useful when new kinds must be added separately.

cards.question: Why are minutes and steps different operations on the same tree?
cards.answer: Minutes measures duration; steps counts leaves. A zero-minute leaf contributes zero to one and one to the other, exposing assumptions hidden by ordinary positive examples.

cards.question: What test detects accidentally counting groups as steps?
cards.answer: Nest an empty group and a one-leaf group inside a parent. The leaf count should be one, regardless of the number of internal groups.

cards.question: Why does reversing two wrappers often change the result?
cards.answer: Each wrapper receives the result of its inner object. Limiting before adding text differs from limiting after adding it, so the composition is generally order-sensitive.

cards.question: Does Decorator require every wrapper to add characters?
cards.answer: No. Limit removes characters while keeping the Message interface. The common property is wrapping an object and changing behavior, not always increasing output size.

cards.question: Why are wrapper service objects nonmovable while their unique_ptr handles can move?
cards.answer: Moving the handle transfers ownership without relocating the service object. This preserves object identity and avoids supporting partially moved service states.

cards.question: Could one formatting function replace this wrapper graph?
cards.answer: Yes for a small fixed pipeline. Wrappers earn their cost when callers assemble and reorder optional behavior through a shared interface.

cards.question: Why should a null-inner check run during construction?
cards.answer: It prevents creating a wrapper that can never satisfy text(). Detecting the error at assembly time is clearer than crashing during a later render.

cards.question: How would byte limits differ from display-character limits?
cards.answer: std::string::substr counts bytes. A UTF-8 character can use several bytes, so a byte cut may split it. A display-text contract needs a suitable text-aware representation.

cards.question: What ownership action happens when the outermost wrapper is destroyed?
cards.answer: Its unique_ptr destroys the inner object, which destroys its own inner object in turn. Virtual destructors allow deletion through Message to reach the actual types.

cards.answer: Seven is in range, but the complete token is not an integer. Syntax validation must establish full consumption before numeric range validation is meaningful.

cards.question: Does a Facade forbid clients from using subsystem classes directly?
cards.answer: No. It offers a simpler supported route. Direct calls may be useful but must respect the subsystem preconditions, such as validating values before summarizing.

cards.question: Why is mean implemented through run rather than duplicating parsing?
cards.answer: run already coordinates syntax, count and range checks. Reusing it keeps a new operation from silently accepting inputs that the old operation rejects.

cards.question: What prevents total overflow under this example's stated bounds?
cards.answer: At most one thousand values each lie between minus one hundred and one hundred. The total magnitude is at most one hundred thousand, which fits the required int implementation used here.

cards.question: What test should accompany an increased input-count limit?
cards.answer: Recheck arithmetic bounds and memory behavior, not only the new count boundary. A previously safe accumulator may become unsafe when the accepted domain grows.

cards.question: Would a single import function be an acceptable facade?
cards.answer: Yes. A facade is an easier entry point over coordinated operations; it need not be a stateful class when a function expresses that job clearly.

cards.question: Why can a successful mean test miss malformed-token bugs?
cards.answer: An ordinary numeric string never exercises the parser's end pointer. Test junk suffixes and fractional tokens separately from arithmetic results.

cards.question: Can clearing the pool guarantee immediate destruction of every style?
cards.answer: No. Marks may still own shared references. Clearing drops only the pool's ownership, and each style dies when its last owner releases it.

cards.question: Why is shared_ptr<const Style> preferable to shared_ptr<Style> here?
cards.answer: Clients should not mutate a style shared by many marks. The const target blocks ordinary mutation through those handles and protects the meaning of the pool key.

cards.question: Does an equal style value imply an equal pointer after clear?

cards.question: When is Flyweight a poor tradeoff?
cards.answer: When there are few repetitions or small cheap values. Maps, pointers and allocation overhead can cost more than storing the data directly; measure the actual workload.

cards.question: Why does std::move(left) still leave this Mark usable in the supplied program?
cards.answer: Mark declares copy operations and no move constructor. The rvalue binds to its copy constructor, which copies the shared pointer and position; std::move alone does not perform a move.

cards.question: What should a memory test measure besides pool.count()?
cards.answer: Count retained styles and client references over time. A small current pool does not imply little live memory if old marks keep earlier styles alive.

cards.question: Why must permission be checked before consulting a populated cache?
cards.answer: A cached value is still protected information. Returning it first would let a client read after access was revoked.

cards.question: What is the difference between unloaded and uncached here?
cards.answer: Unloaded means no RealHours object exists. Uncached means no remembered opening value exists. Invalidation can clear the value while retaining the already constructed service.

cards.question: Why use optional<int> instead of zero as the empty-cache marker?
cards.answer: Midnight is a valid zero opening hour. optional represents absence separately from all valid integer values.

cards.question: Does caching promise that opening always returns current source data?
cards.answer: No. This proxy explicitly allows staleness until invalidate or refresh. Freshness is part of the contract and must be clear to callers.

cards.question: When would direct access be simpler than this proxy?
cards.answer: When source reads are cheap and no caching, delayed construction or access control is needed. An extra proxy then adds state without solving a real problem.

cards.question: Why does a denied refresh leave the old cache intact?
cards.answer: Permission is tested before invalidation. A rejected request must not change the cache or perform a source read under this contract.

cards.question: What lifetime issue is not solved by owning RealHours?

cards.answer: An empty optional means decline and continue. A present empty string is still a reply and stops the chain, so the representation separates absence from reply content.

cards.question: Why put page validation before the handler loop?
cards.answer: The input rule applies to all destinations. Without one shared gate, an early permissive rule might accept a request that later rules would reject.

cards.question: When would a map from format to handler be simpler?
cards.answer: When formats are distinct keys with no overlap or priority. A chain is useful when multiple rules can match and ordered choice is intentional.

cards.question: What regression test should accompany inserting a broad handler near the front?
cards.answer: Check requests previously handled by later specific rules. A broad match can shadow them even when its own isolated tests pass.

cards.question: Does this chain call every accepting handler?
cards.answer: No. It returns at the first present Reply. A broadcast pipeline is a different contract and needs different control flow and tests.

cards.question: Why is a vector of functions sufficient for this example?
cards.answer: Each rule has one operation and needs no exposed object state. A class hierarchy would add machinery without improving this small callable contract.

cards.question: What should happen if a Rule itself throws?
cards.answer: The supplied route does not catch it, so the exception propagates and later handlers do not run. Continuing after failure would require an explicit error policy.

cards.question: Why must rollback run in reverse execution order?
cards.answer: Each command saved the receiver value produced by earlier commands. Reversing unwinds those dependent changes back to the original state.

cards.question: Does run_batch roll back every possible exception?
cards.answer: No. It catches out_of_range only and assumes undo succeeds for its intended Move commands. A general transaction system needs policies for other failures and failed undo.

cards.question: Why does constructing Move leave Marker unchanged?
cards.answer: A Command represents a request before executing it. Separating creation from execution allows queuing and inspection without immediate side effects.

cards.question: What keeps a queued Move's receiver alive?
cards.answer: The caller's lifetime discipline. Move holds Marker by reference, so the marker must outlive queued execution and any later undo.

cards.question: Why set applied only after marker.set succeeds?
cards.answer: A rejected target must not mark the command as applied. Otherwise undo could pretend to reverse a change that never occurred.

cards.question: Could a lambda replace Command for a fire-and-forget action?
cards.answer: Yes. The interface is useful when the caller needs shared operations such as execute and undo. A single callable can be simpler when undo and stored status are unnecessary.

cards.question: What additional test is needed for a batch starting from position one?
cards.answer: Fail after two successful moves and assert rollback reaches one, not zero. This catches implementations that reset to a hard-coded default instead of restoring history.

cards.question: Why copy the current element out of Cursor::read?
cards.answer: The caller receives an int value rather than a reference into vector storage. A later append cannot invalidate that copied number, though it invalidates the cursor.

cards.question: Does the version stamp keep a destroyed Readings owner alive?
cards.answer: No. It detects mutations only while the borrowed owner is alive. Using a cursor after owner destruction is still invalid.

cards.question: Why validate done as well as read?
cards.answer: A stale cursor must not silently appear finished or unfinished against a changed collection. Every operation that observes traversal state must respect invalidation.

cards.question: Would standard vector iterators be preferable in ordinary code?
cards.answer: Usually, if their invalidation rules satisfy the requirement. This custom cursor adds a checked version contract for teaching and for clients needing explicit stale-view errors.

cards.question: Why check version exhaustion before appending?
cards.answer: The version must never wrap to an old value and falsely validate a stale cursor. The check prevents mutation when no fresh stamp is available.

cards.question: What does independent position mean when two cursors share one owner?
cards.answer: They read the same collection but track separate indices. Advancing one cursor must not advance the other; appending to the owner invalidates both.

cards.question: Why use remaining minus one for reverse read?
cards.answer: remaining counts unread elements. For a nonempty view, the next reverse index is one less than that count; checking empty first prevents unsigned underflow.

cards.question: Why are silent button updates important?
cards.answer: If enabling the button emitted another change that repeated coordination, it could form a feedback loop. The mediator updates derived state without recursively notifying itself.

cards.question: What invariant should a table-driven test cover?
cards.answer: For all combinations, enabled equals nonempty name AND accepted consent AND no hold. Testing the truth table catches accidentally dropped conditions.

cards.question: Could Form become too large as fields grow?
cards.answer: Yes. A mediator reduces links among controls but can collect too much policy. Split independent coordination responsibilities when they no longer belong to one coherent form rule.

cards.question: Why is copying Form forbidden?
cards.answer: NameField stores a reference to its mediator. A naive copy could leave the copied field reporting to the original form instead of its new owner.

cards.question: When would direct field interaction be simpler?
cards.answer: For two controls with one stable rule and no growing web of dependencies. Central coordination becomes valuable as several inputs jointly determine behavior.

cards.question: Why does History store snapshots instead of accessing Selection's private fields?
cards.answer: Selection owns the rule for creating valid saved state. History can keep and return opaque values without learning or duplicating that internal representation.

cards.question: Is this snapshot tied to the identity of one Selection object?
cards.answer: No. It holds a valid interval pair and can restore another Selection. An identity-bound snapshot would need a different contract and checks.

cards.question: Why copy the history before eviction and insertion?
cards.answer: If allocation fails while building the proposed history, the original history remains unchanged. Evicting first would lose an entry before the new one was safely stored.

cards.question: What happens when undo succeeds?
cards.answer: The most recent snapshot restores the selection, then that history entry is removed. A second undo moves to an older entry rather than repeating the same restore forever.

cards.question: When can saving a whole object be too expensive?
cards.answer: When state is very large or changes frequently. Deltas, persistent structures or explicit commands may reduce storage, at the cost of more complex restore behavior.

cards.question: What distinguishes Memento from Command undo in these chapters?
cards.answer: Memento restores saved state. Command remembers an operation and enough information to reverse it. Both can support undo but store different kinds of history.

cards.question: Why validate a pair before assigning either endpoint?

cards.question: Does a throwing listener undo earlier deliveries?
cards.answer: No. Total changes its sum before its hook, and earlier listeners may already have run. The exception stops later delivery but does not roll back completed effects.

cards.question: Why store weak_ptr registrations instead of shared_ptr registrations?
cards.answer: The feed does not own listener lifetime. A client can release its listener without a permanent feed reference keeping it alive.

cards.question: What keeps a listener alive during one update call?
cards.answer: Locking its weak_ptr produces a temporary shared_ptr. That temporary keeps the listener alive for the call even if other owners release it meanwhile.

cards.question: How does the older snapshot-policy lab differ from Feed?
cards.answer: The snapshot lab copies its listener list before dispatch. Feed instead rejects registration changes during dispatch. These are alternative policies, not conflicting guarantees of Observer itself.

cards.question: Why forbid nested publish in this Feed?
cards.answer: Nested delivery can create unexpected order and recursive calls. This example chooses a simple nonreentrant contract and reports the attempt instead of pretending to support it.

cards.question: What must a cleanup guard restore after callback failure?
cards.answer: The notifying flag. Without scope-based cleanup, one exception would leave the feed permanently busy even though no delivery is active.

cards.question: Does weak_ptr make concurrent subscribe and publish safe?
cards.answer: No. It manages lifetime, not unsynchronized access to the registration vector and flag. This example does not provide a multithreaded publication contract.

cards.question: Why does next return a proposed state rather than delete the current state itself?
cards.answer: The current virtual call must finish before its object is destroyed. Session receives the proposal and only then replaces its owning pointer.

cards.question: What distinguishes an invalid event from a self-transition here?
cards.answer: An invalid event returns no proposal and send returns false. The context remains unchanged without constructing a replacement object.

cards.question: Could an enum and switch be simpler for three states?
cards.answer: Yes. This hierarchy demonstrates delegating behavior to state objects. For a small stable transition table, an enum can be clearer and require fewer allocations.

cards.question: Why does the capstone's enum not automatically make it the State pattern?
cards.answer: A state machine describes permitted transitions. The object-oriented State pattern specifically delegates state-dependent behavior to state objects; the capstone uses explicit guards instead.

cards.question: What test distinguishes cancel from finish?
cards.answer: Begin, then cancel, and assert idle; begin, then finish, and assert done. Both stop active work but permit different next events.

cards.question: Why keep state_ private to Session?
cards.answer: The context must control replacement timing and preserve its nonnull current state. Exposing the owner lets callers bypass transition rules or clear it.

cards.question: What should happen if allocation of a proposed state fails?
cards.answer: The exception propagates before replacement, leaving the current owned state intact. The caller can report failure without claiming the transition completed.

cards.question: Is runtime polymorphism required for every strategy choice?
cards.answer: No. A function, callable parameter or compile-time policy can be simpler. An owned virtual strategy fits this example because callers replace behavior at runtime through one interface.

cards.question: Why validate a new strategy before assigning rule_?

cards.question: What separates Strategy from State here?
cards.answer: The client selects an algorithm for the same task. There is no state-transition protocol that chooses the next behavior based on events.

cards.question: Why test both even and odd sample counts for Middle?

cards.question: Does the average's integer result round to nearest?

cards.question: Why validate converted output if raw input was valid?
cards.answer: A derived hook can still violate its contract. BrokenImport demonstrates that valid raw input alone does not guarantee a valid result.

cards.question: Could passing a conversion callable be simpler than inheritance?
cards.answer: Yes, especially for one small varying step. Template Method is useful when a base workflow coordinates several overridable steps or an existing inheritance framework requires them.

cards.question: Why should expected-output comparison preserve the trailing space?
cards.answer: The supplied formatter intentionally emits it. Trimming output can hide formatting regressions and make the printed contract differ from what the program actually returns.

cards.question: Does const run forbid changes anywhere in the program?
cards.answer: No. It constrains ordinary mutation through this object. A derived hook could still touch mutable or external state; such effects need their own documented contract.

cards.question: What regression test protects a new subclass from bypassing input rules?
cards.answer: Call it with empty input and with 101, and require the same base exceptions as older subclasses. Successful new output alone does not verify the inherited gates.

cards.question: Visitor: Bolt price. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.answer: 20. The Bolts visit multiplies count by five cents.

cards.question: Visitor: Cable price. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.answer: 120. The Cable visit uses forty cents per metre.

cards.question: Visitor: Mixed accumulation. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.code: ([]{ Price p; Bolts(4).accept(p); Cable(3).accept(p); return p.cents(); })()
cards.answer: 140. A single visitor accumulates both visits in order.

cards.question: Visitor: Zero quantity. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.answer: 0. Zero is a valid quantity that adds no cost.

cards.question: Visitor: Bolt label. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.answer: "bolts=4". The overload for Bolts emits the bolt-count label.

cards.question: Visitor: Cable label. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.answer: "cable-m=3". The overload for Cable names metres, not bolts.

cards.question: Visitor: Label order. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.code: ([]{ Labels l; Cable(2).accept(l); Bolts(1).accept(l); return l.lines.at(0)+"|"+l.lines.at(1); })()
cards.answer: "cable-m=2|bolts=1". The visitor preserves the order in which elements accept it.

cards.question: Visitor: Invalid cable length. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.answer: true. Element validation remains in the element type, independent of each visitor.

cards.question: Visitor: diagnose this replacement line in the extended implementation. Which contract does it break?
cards.answer: Visitor overloads encode distinct prices: cables cost forty cents per metre. Correct excerpt: cable.metres() * 40

cards.question: Visitor: diagnose this replacement line in the extended implementation. Which contract does it break?
cards.answer: The Labels overload must preserve the type-specific unit in its output. Correct excerpt: "cable-m=" + std::to_string(cable.metres())

cards.question: Why does visitor.visit(*this) choose a type-specific overload inside accept?
cards.answer: Inside Bolts::accept, *this has the Bolts type. Overload selection identifies visit(Bolts), then virtual dispatch chooses that operation's implementation on the actual visitor.

cards.question: What becomes expensive when adding a new Part kind?
cards.answer: Every Visitor implementation must support the new visit overload. Visitor favors adding operations over adding element types frequently.

cards.question: Why is adding Labels cheaper than editing every element's formatting method?
cards.answer: Labels adds a separate operation through the existing accept interface. Bolts and Cable need no new formatting-specific fields or methods.

cards.question: Can the same Price instance be reused for several parts?
cards.answer: Yes; it intentionally accumulates cents. Use a fresh visitor when a new independent total is required, or add an explicit reset contract.

cards.question: Why check the remaining price capacity before addition?
cards.answer: The one-million-cent limit is part of the visitor invariant. Rejection must leave the accumulated total unchanged instead of accepting a partial or wrapped value.

cards.question: Would a switch over a variant be a reasonable alternative?
cards.answer: Yes for a closed set of value-like element kinds. Both approaches make operations handle each kind; their maintenance costs differ in allocation, extensibility and compiler support.

cards.question: Why keep quantity validation in Bolts and Cable rather than Price?
cards.answer: Validity of an element must hold for every operation, including Labels. Putting it only in Price would let invalid elements reach other visitors.

cards.question: Capstone: combine patterns in a complete system: Fahrenheit freezing. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.answer: true. Subtract thirty-two before multiplying by five ninths.

cards.question: Capstone: combine patterns in a complete system: Fahrenheit boiling. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.answer: true. The normalized sample is one hundred Celsius before any alert rule runs.

cards.question: Capstone: combine patterns in a complete system: Late bad sample rollback. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.code: ([]{ Monitor m(std::make_unique<AtLeast>(80)); m.start(); m.ingest({{1,20,'C'}}); const bool bad=dpx_rejects<std::invalid_argument>([&]{m.ingest({{2,30,'C'},{3,40,'K'}});}); return bad && m.records().size()==1; })()
cards.answer: true. A private staged vector absorbs the valid prefix and is discarded when the last unit is invalid.

cards.question: Capstone: combine patterns in a complete system: Duplicate ID rollback. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.code: ([]{ Monitor m(std::make_unique<AtLeast>(80)); m.start(); const bool bad=dpx_rejects<std::invalid_argument>([&]{m.ingest({{1,20,'C'},{1,30,'C'}});}); return bad && m.records().empty(); })()
cards.answer: true. Ordering is checked against the staged history; a duplicate invalidates the whole batch.

cards.question: Capstone: combine patterns in a complete system: Band low endpoint. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.answer: false. The lower endpoint is inside the safe interval.

cards.question: Capstone: combine patterns in a complete system: Band high endpoint. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.answer: false. The upper endpoint is also safe; only values above it alert.

cards.question: Capstone: combine patterns in a complete system: Outside band. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.answer: true. Either side outside the closed safe interval triggers an alert.

cards.question: Capstone: combine patterns in a complete system: Rule change preserves history. What does this expression return? Use the extended chapter implementation in the linked lab. dpx_rejects<E> returns true only if its callable throws E.
cards.code: ([]{ Monitor m(std::make_unique<OutsideBand>(20,60)); m.start(); m.ingest({{1,61,'C'}}); m.pause(); m.replace_rule(std::make_unique<AtLeast>(100)); m.resume(); m.ingest({{2,61,'C'}}); return m.records()[0].alert && !m.records()[1].alert; })()
cards.answer: true. The old record stores its old decision; only the newly ingested record uses the replacement rule.

cards.question: Why must unit conversion happen before the alert strategy?
cards.answer: The strategy contract uses Celsius. Comparing raw Fahrenheit with a Celsius threshold can produce a plausible but false alert decision.

cards.question: Does a valid prefix of a batch become visible before a bad final record?
cards.answer: No. Monitor stages a private copy and commits only after the entire batch passes. A late error must leave the public record vector unchanged.

cards.question: Why compare a new ID with staged.back rather than only the old history?
cards.answer: The staged vector includes earlier records in the same batch. Checking only old history would miss duplicate or decreasing IDs within the new batch.

cards.question: Why retain the bool alert in each Record instead of recomputing it in reports?
cards.answer: It records the policy decision made at intake. Recomputing after a strategy change would rewrite the meaning of historical records.

cards.question: What is the safe meaning of a band with equal endpoints?
cards.answer: Only that exact Celsius value is inside the safe band. Values below or above it alert; equality itself does not.

cards.question: Why permit rule replacement only while idle or paused?
cards.answer: The contract gives changes a clear boundary between intake periods. A running replacement would make the policy timing harder to reason about.

cards.question: Does the state enum implement the polymorphic State pattern?
cards.answer: No. It supports an explicit state machine with guards. The capstone intentionally uses the simpler form while combining Adapter, Strategy and Facade responsibilities.

cards.question: What survives a failed null replacement while paused?
cards.answer: The old owned rule and all records remain. Check the proposed pointer before assigning it so a rejected change cannot disable future intake.

cards.question: Why is a reference to the records vector different from a reference to one element?
cards.answer: The vector object remains a member of Monitor. Commit swaps its storage, which can invalidate references to old elements; a reference to the vector object still names that member.

cards.question: What does noexcept on AlertRule::alert promise?
cards.answer: An implementation must not let an exception escape. Violating that promise terminates the program; it is not a mechanism for safely catching arbitrary strategy errors.

cards.question: Why does ReportFacade use the classic locale?
cards.answer: The printed decimal separator must match the recorded output regardless of a user's locale. Stable formatting makes exact verification meaningful.

cards.question: Can successful output alone prove the batch guarantee?
cards.answer: No. Test a batch with an early valid item and a late invalid one, then compare the complete previous report. Success cases do not exercise partial-commit risks.

cards.question: Why should adapter tests include invalid units and nonfinite values?
cards.answer: An unknown unit or NaN can bypass ordinary threshold intuition. The normalization boundary must reject values that cannot satisfy the sensor domain.

cards.question: What should an eighth stored record do compared with a ninth?
cards.answer: The eighth fits the fixed capacity; a ninth is rejected before any history change. Capacity is a domain rule here, not a claim that vector cannot grow.

cards.question: Why keep ownership tests when every current strategy has no resource besides numbers?
cards.answer: Future strategies may hold resources. Deleting through AlertRule must still call the actual destructor when replacing a rule or destroying Monitor.

cards.question: When would copying the whole history stop being an appropriate transaction method?
cards.answer: When histories become large or throughput matters. A bounded eight-record example makes copying simple; larger systems may stage only new data or use another commit representation.

cards.question: Why is stop final rather than another kind of pause?
cards.answer: The state contract provides resume only from paused. A stopped monitor cannot restart; a new session requires a new object.

cards.question: What integration test distinguishes old and new policy decisions on equal temperatures?
cards.answer: Ingest 61 under OutsideBand(20,60), pause and select AtLeast(100), then ingest 61 again. The first record alerts and the second does not, proving historical decisions persist.

before.title: Pattern overview
paragraphs: Factory Method lets a stable operation request an object while a subclass chooses its concrete type. The attached chapter begins with transport choices and later uses dialog buttons. Those settings lead to the same design question: how can a workflow use a product without fixing its concrete class?

The creator declares a virtual creation operation returning the product interface. Its ordinary workflow calls that operation and then uses the returned product. A concrete creator overrides the creation operation. The important change is the path of the call: existing workflow code reaches the subclass through virtual dispatch. before.title: Two connected type families, one clear handoff
paragraphs: TextJob and BracketJob derive from ArchiveJob. TextRecord and BracketRecord derive from Record. These are separate relationships. A TextJob is a kind of ArchiveJob; it is not a kind of TextRecord. The job creates the record and then uses it through the Record interface. Confusing those relationships leads to misleading class diagrams and often to bad code.

The protected make declaration returns unique_ptr<Record>. Each override keeps that return type and constructs its concrete class with make_unique. A unique_ptr<TextRecord> can transfer into unique_ptr<Record> when the pointer conversion and deleter requirements are met. This is ownership conversion, not virtual return-type covariance. C++ covariant overrides apply to certain raw pointer and reference return types, not to arbitrary smart-pointer templates.

run receives the owning handle in a local variable. It checks the non-null postcondition, calls format, builds its result string, and leaves scope. The local handle then destroys the product. Returning the string does not extend the product lifetime because the string owns its own characters. If format throws, cleanup still releases the record. The virtual Record destructor is essential for complete destruction through a base owning handle.

before.title: Compilation fixes the request; execution chooses the maker
paragraphs: The compiler checks that ArchiveJob declares make and that each override matches it. At execution, the object on which run was called determines which make override runs. Calling run through const ArchiveJob& selected still reaches BracketJob::make when selected refers to the bracket job. A reference changes what operations the caller can name; it does not erase the actual object type.

The call to make happens after label validation. An empty or oversized label therefore creates no product. Once a product exists, its format method is another virtual call. The sequence is shared validation, virtual creation, virtual formatting, then shared receipt assembly. Factory Method is often one specialized step inside a Template Method-style workflow, but the terms describe different decisions: one concerns object creation; the other concerns algorithm order.

A null result is a broken creator contract, so the job throws logic_error. EmptyJob exists only to verify that guard. An allocation failure can also occur inside make_unique and propagate as an exception; no successfully constructed handle exists to leak. For a real file-backed product, document whether creation opens a file, delays opening, or can reuse a resource. The pattern alone says nothing about those effects.

before.title: What does not make a Factory Method
paragraphs: A free function make_record(format) with a switch is commonly called a simple factory. It centralizes construction and may be exactly what a program needs. It is not this pattern’s defining mechanism because no inherited workflow calls an overridable creation hook. A static member named create is not automatically Factory Method either. Names do not decide a design pattern; relationships and control flow do.

If the caller can supply a ready-made Record, dependency injection is often simpler than subclassing ArchiveJob. If the workflow needs a fresh record for every run, it can accept a callable factory. Factory Method fits best when creator inheritance already has a clear role and subclasses should choose products. Avoid introducing two class hierarchies solely to hide one constructor.

New product behavior still needs interface-level tests. A new format that silently truncates labels could satisfy the C++ signature and still violate requirements. Likewise, switching the product does not make the stored prefix truthful about persistent storage. Keep the workflow’s externally promised behavior explicit, and test it through the base creator interface so extensions exercise the same path clients will use.

discussion.question: Why is choosing an encoder and decoder independently risky, even when each one works alone?
discussion.answer: Their wire formats may disagree. A framed encoder can produce [7] while a plain decoder expects 7. The requirement is a matching pair, not merely two individually valid objects.

before.title: The failure is a mismatched pair
paragraphs: When framed connections arrive, setup code selects both products independently. A copied branch can create FramedEncoder with PlainDecoder. Both objects implement the right C++ interfaces, so the compiler accepts the code. The encoder produces [7], but the plain decoder rejects its length. A more permissive decoder might silently misread the data instead. The problem is agreement between products, not merely selecting one product.

A family is a set of objects meant to work together. The Abstract Factory pattern gives the caller one object that creates all needed members of the selected family. CodecFactory offers encoder and decoder. PlainFactory creates the plain pair; FramedFactory creates the framed pair. The client chooses one factory, then asks that factory for both products. This reduces the number of places where incompatible choices can enter.

after.title: The failure is a mismatched pair
paragraphs: When framed connections arrive, setup code selects both products independently. A copied branch can create FramedEncoder with PlainDecoder. Both objects implement the right C++ interfaces, so the compiler accepts the code. The encoder produces [7], but the plain decoder rejects its length. A more permissive decoder might silently misread the data instead. The problem is agreement between products, not merely selecting one product.

A family is a set of objects meant to work together. The Abstract Factory pattern gives the caller one object that creates all needed members of the selected family. CodecFactory offers encoder and decoder. PlainFactory creates the plain pair; FramedFactory creates the framed pair. The client chooses one factory, then asks that factory for both products. This reduces the number of places where incompatible choices can enter.

before.title: Two product roles are not one inheritance tree
paragraphs: Encoder and Decoder have different operations, so they remain different interfaces. PlainEncoder and FramedEncoder implement Encoder. PlainDecoder and FramedDecoder implement Decoder. Each concrete factory creates one of each. Abstract Factory does not require these two products to inherit from each other, share a common catch-all interface, or own one another. Their useful relationship is a protocol contract: decoder.read(encoder.write(value)) equals value for every valid value.

The factory itself is borrowed as const CodecFactory&. The client does not delete it and does not save its address. Each returned unique_ptr owns a fresh product. The products contain no reference back to the factory, so this implementation does not require them to die before the factory. In round_trip they are local and are destroyed when the call ends. A different implementation with shared factory state would need a documented lifetime rule instead of assuming this one applies.

The compiler checks product method signatures and factory overrides. During execution, the actual factory type chooses the concrete products. Calling through Encoder and Decoder then chooses their actual method implementations. The client contains no switch on wire format. It still knows the abstract protocol duties: one writer, one reader, a valid integer, and a round-trip invariant.

before.title: Parsing is part of the contract
paragraphs: PlainDecoder checks that wire has exactly one character before testing its content. The || operator stops as soon as an operand is true. This short-circuit rule skips unnecessary content tests after a bad length. FramedDecoder uses the same ordering for a stronger safety reason: front() and back() require a nonempty string. Its size check rejects empty input before either operation can run. C++17 permits reading string[string.size()] as a zero character, so PlainDecoder’s wire[0] on an empty string is not the same invalid-access case as front() or back().

The character tests compare the input with '0' and '9'. C++ guarantees the decimal digit characters form a consecutive sequence, so subtracting '0' from a checked digit yields its numeric value. The framed reader first checks a three-character shape with opening and closing brackets. Only then does it take the one-character substring and reuse PlainDecoder. That reuse is a local parsing dependency, not membership in the plain factory family.

The encoder checks numeric range before making a string. The framed decoder rejects [x] even though its outer brackets are correct. Structural validity and content validity are different rules. These deliberately tiny formats let the tests cover all ten accepted numeric values. They are teaching protocols, not general-purpose serialization formats with escaping, byte-order rules, versioning, or checksums.

before.title: A factory encourages compatibility; it does not prove it
paragraphs: Nothing in the return types prevents a faulty FramedFactory from returning PlainDecoder. The family rule is a design contract backed by tests. round_trip checks the value after decoding. That catches mismatches or broken decoding for the tested values. It cannot certify all future protocol extensions by itself. If a family has many configuration values, test representative boundaries and generated cases, and consider carrying a shared immutable configuration object into both products.

A factory is most useful when clients need several related product roles and whole families change together. Adding a new family is local: provide its products and a factory implementing the existing creation operations. Adding a new product role is less local: a new creation method affects every factory and every family. This is the pattern’s main change-direction tradeoff. Choose it when new families are more likely than new roles.

For one encoder-decoder pair with no planned variants, direct construction is clearer. A function returning a struct containing both owning handles can also preserve pairing with less inheritance. Compile-time family types or a single codec object can enforce stronger relationships when runtime variation is unnecessary. Do not split one naturally cohesive codec into separate products solely to make an Abstract Factory diagram. Here separate send and receive components are the stated need; the factory coordinates their creation.

before.title: Pattern overview
paragraphs: Builder separates the steps that assemble a product from the completed product itself. The attached chapter motivates this with many house options and later shows vehicle/manual representations. The problem is a growing construction process, rather than choosing a single class with one call.

A builder retains work between construction steps. A director can package a repeatable sequence of those steps, while the client obtains the finished result from the builder. Different builders can interpret the same steps to produce different representations; their products need not share a base class. A chain of calls is optional syntax. The lasting design distinction is the separate construction process and product.

before.title: The plan has rules that span several inputs
paragraphs: A teaching session planner needs a title and between one and three timed activities. Each activity lasts from 1 through 60 minutes, and the whole plan lasts no more than 90 minutes. A valid plan can be handed to a presenter. An unfinished draft cannot. The title and durations arrive in separate setup steps, perhaps from a form or a configuration reader.

The simplest implementation is a struct with a title and a vector of minutes. Fill the fields and then call validate before using it. That can be enough in a short local function. The difficulty appears when the draft escapes to other code before validation or when one caller forgets the check. The same type then means both “possibly incomplete” and “safe to present.”

discussion.question: Why should an unfinished draft not already count as a valid Plan?
discussion.answer: A draft may lack a title or activities, or its final duration may exceed ninety minutes. A finished Plan should promise those rules already hold, so the program needs a clear completion check.

before.title: Separate the draft from the finished product
paragraphs: A builder is an object that gathers construction choices in steps and produces a usable product when those choices are complete. This is the Builder pattern. PlanBuilder can be incomplete. Plan cannot be created through the public interface until build succeeds. The design makes the boundary visible: collecting settings is different from possessing a valid plan.

named sets a nonempty title. add accepts one valid activity while respecting the three-activity limit. build checks rules that need the whole draft: a title exists, at least one activity exists, and the sum is at most 90. A draft with two 60-minute activities can exist, but build rejects it. That is deliberate; intermediate choices are not claimed to be a finished plan. A form could let a user edit such a draft before trying again.

before.title: Why friendship is narrow here
paragraphs: Plan has a private constructor and private data. friend class PlanBuilder grants this one named class access to the private constructor. Friendship is permission, not inheritance, ownership, or automatic trust in every caller. It is not symmetric or transitive. The builder is responsible for checking its draft before using that permission. No other public function in this example can create an invalid Plan by filling fields afterward.

The finished Plan exposes a title reference for reading and a computed total. Its public interface has no setters. Calling title returns a borrowed const string reference, valid only while that Plan remains alive and unchanged by assignment or movement. Returning a copy would provide a simpler lifetime contract at the cost of copying the title. Do not retain the borrowed reference after the plan dies.

build returns Plan by value. The constructor receives a string and vector by value and moves those parameters into its members. Because build itself is const and passes its own members as lvalues, the constructor parameters are copies of the draft. The resulting plan therefore owns independent data. Later builder changes cannot alter earlier products. Plan explicitly defaults its copy constructor. This suppresses implicit move operations, so constructing or assigning it from an rvalue uses copying instead and leaves the source valid. Moving the builder’s temporary constructor parameters into the new product is still safe: those parameters are ordinary local values, not previously published plans. C++17 can construct the returned product directly in its destination; correctness must not depend on counting visible copy calls.

before.title: Chaining steps does not create magic
paragraphs: named and add return PlanBuilder&, a reference to the same builder. return *this dereferences the implicit this pointer to refer to the current object. This supports builder.named("Practice").add(30).add(30): each call returns the object on which the next call operates. Chaining is an optional convenience. It is not what makes the design Builder; staged construction and the valid-product boundary are the important parts.

The member functions check invalid values before changing their vectors or titles. A rejected add(0) leaves the existing draft unchanged. A fourth activity is rejected even if it would fit the time total, because count and total are separate rules. The maximum sum of a draft is 180, so this example’s int arithmetic cannot overflow on the required compiler platform. A production planner with unbounded counts needs a different bound or checked accumulation.

The program demonstrates two snapshots from one builder. After 30 and 30, first totals 60. Adding another 30 produces second at 90. first still totals 60 because it owns its own copied durations. build does not reset the builder in this design. That policy is part of its contract, not a universal rule. A consuming builder might move data out and require a reset; a reusable builder might return snapshots, as ours does.

before.title: A director is just a reusable recipe
paragraphs: introduction records a repeated sequence of builder calls. Such a recipe is called a director in the classic Builder vocabulary. A director does not have to be a class. Here an ordinary function creates a builder, names the plan, adds two activities, and returns the result. The caller receives a Plan without knowing every construction step. If no recipe repeats, callers can drive the builder directly.

The broader Builder pattern can use one recipe with different builders to produce different representations, such as an executable session plan and a printed outline. Those products need not share a base type. A common step interface can express named and add, while each concrete builder exposes its own finished result. A function template can also apply one recipe to builders with matching operations. Introduce that machinery only when the second representation exists; one valid-plan builder does not need an abstract builder hierarchy.

For a small object with two required values available at once, a checked constructor or a named factory function is simpler. A builder becomes valuable when many optional choices accumulate, validation spans choices, or setup order and product readiness need clear separation. before.title: Pattern overview
paragraphs: Prototype copies an already configured object without requiring its caller to know the object's concrete class. The attached chapter distinguishes this active copying role from a rough early product model. Its object-copying problem is the same one our cue collection faces: the caller has a base interface, yet the copy must preserve the actual kind of object.

The base interface declares a virtual clone operation. Each concrete implementation creates its own concrete type using the current object as the source of values. The caller invokes clone through the base interface and receives a new object. A registry can hold named prototypes for reuse, but the registry is optional. The copy policy must say which data becomes independent and which resources, if any, remain shared.

before.question: What is Prototype?
before.answer: A pattern in which an existing object creates a new object by copying its own state through a common operation.

before.question: What is Object slicing?
before.answer: Losing the derived part when a derived object is copied into a base value.

before.question: What is Deep copy?
before.answer: A copy that duplicates owned contents to the independence depth required by the application.

before.question: What is Shallow copy?
before.answer: A copy that duplicates handles while retaining some shared underlying objects.

before.question: Why is copying the unique_ptr address into another owning handle not cloning?
before.answer: Both handles would own the same object, leading to double deletion. clone must create a distinct object with the promised copied state.

before.question: Is a prototype registry required for the cue example?
before.answer: No. The collection already supplies each source object. A registry becomes useful when callers need to look up configured prototypes by a key.

before.title: The limitation is lost concrete type information
paragraphs: A unique_ptr cannot be copied because copying the sole owner would give two owners responsibility for deleting one object. Copying Cue itself would not solve the problem either. Cue is abstract here, so it cannot be constructed. In a nonabstract hierarchy, copying only the base part can discard derived data and behavior, a problem called object slicing. Neither copying the handle nor copying only the base subobject means “make an independent object of the same actual kind.”

The Prototype pattern asks the existing object to create that copy. Cue declares a virtual clone operation returning a new owning Cue handle. TextCue and ListCue each know their own concrete type, so each can call its own copy constructor. The caller asks for a clone without deciding which constructor to invoke. Prototype is therefore about construction from an existing object’s state, not simply about any function named copy.

before.title: What clone preserves
paragraphs: ListCue::clone calls make_unique<ListCue>(*this). this points at the current ListCue; *this refers to the whole current ListCue object. Inside a const member, that expression is a const reference suitable for copying. The explicitly defaulted copy constructor copies the vector member. Both concrete cue types declare their copy constructors this way, suppressing implicit object moves. Constructing from an rvalue therefore copies instead of emptying the source; moves of unique_ptr handles still transfer ownership without moving the cue object itself. Copying a vector of strings copies each string value, so the clone owns independent character data in the normal observable sense. Editing one list’s first name does not edit the other list’s name.

The clone’s type is still ListCue even though its returned owner is unique_ptr<Cue>. Later virtual calls to text and rename reach ListCue behavior. The new object has a different address but starts with the same public value. Equal value and shared identity are different ideas: two clocks can display the same time without being the same clock. The program checks both equal initial text and distinct object addresses.

During compilation, the compiler generates the appropriate memberwise copy constructor and checks the clone override signature. During execution, the actual cue chooses which clone override runs. Allocation creates new storage, construction copies the concrete object into it, and ownership returns to the caller. If copying fails, make_unique cleans up the allocated storage; the original remains owned by its existing handle.

before.title: Copy depth is a design decision
paragraphs: A shallow copy copies a handle or address while keeping the same underlying resource. A deep copy makes an independent copy of owned contents, to the depth promised by the application. The words need a boundary. A vector of strings gives independent string values. A vector of shared_ptr<Image> would copy handles and share images unless the clone explicitly copied them. That may be correct if images are immutable and expensive, but it would not be correct for an independently editable image promise.

A unique_ptr member normally makes the containing type noncopyable until a copy operation is explicitly defined. The lab adds BoxCue with a unique_ptr<string>. Its copy constructor allocates a new string initialized from the original string. Simply returning make_unique<BoxCue>(*this) without that copy constructor would fail to compile. Replacing unique_ptr with shared_ptr just to silence the error would change ownership meaning and make edits visible through both handles.

Some resources should not be cloned at all. A live socket, open transaction, mutex, or hardware session has an identity that copying bytes cannot duplicate. A clone may copy configuration while opening a fresh session, share a documented immutable resource, or reject duplication. Cyclic object graphs need additional rules: a map from old objects to new objects can preserve internal relationships without infinite recursion. Do not promise a universal deep copy without defining where the copy stops.

before.title: Keep the generic loop simple and the copy rules local
paragraphs: The loop over originals uses const auto& because each vector element is a unique_ptr and must not be copied. The reference borrows the owning handle; const prevents reseating that handle through this reference. It does not by itself make the pointed-to object const. clone is separately declared const to promise that cloning does not mutate the cue’s ordinary members. The arrow calls the operation on the object reached through the handle.

Each new owner goes into copies. push_back accepts the returned temporary owning handle by move. After the loop, originals and copies are separate owning collections. Destruction of either collection destroys only its own objects. The program renames the first entry of the copied ListCue and checks that the original text is still list:Check;Begin; while the copied text becomes list:Inspect;Begin;.

Prototype is useful for user duplication, reusable configured objects, and heterogeneous snapshots when copying has a clear domain meaning. A registry may keep named prototypes and return clones, but the registry is optional. If the concrete type is already known and ordinary value copying works, use it. If objects should have unique noncopyable identities, omit clone instead of adding a misleading operation. Maintaining a clone requires adding new fields to its copy policy as the type evolves, especially when members change from values to owning or shared handles.

before.question: What is Singleton?
before.answer: A design that controls access to one instance through a shared accessor.

before.question: What is Mutex?
before.answer: A synchronization object used to allow one participating thread at a time into a protected region.

before.question: What is Critical section?
before.answer: Code that accesses shared state while holding the required lock.

before.question: What is Data race?
before.answer: Unsynchronized conflicting accesses to memory by different threads, with at least one write; in C++ this causes undefined behavior.

before.question: What is Dependency injection?
before.answer: Supplying an object a component needs through an explicit parameter or constructor instead of locating it globally.

before.question: Does a function-local static make next_++ thread-safe?
before.answer: No. It protects initial construction, not later state changes. take must lock its exhaustion check and increment together.

before.question: Why must a test not insist that the safe attached sample always prints FOO twice?
before.answer: Either thread can initialize first. Both values must agree, but the language does not guarantee which input wins the race to acquire the lock.

before.title: One dispenser, not one counter per caller
paragraphs: A small demonstration process issues tickets numbered 1, 2, and 3. Different callers must draw from the same sequence. After the third ticket, every request is rejected. Restarting the process starts a new sequence; the program does not store tickets on disk. This is a deliberately small model of a shared service, not a distributed ticket system.

The simplest good solution is often to create one ordinary dispenser in main and pass a reference to every user. That gives one instance by application arrangement. The excerpt shows a local counter’s core idea, assuming requests are sequential. If separate components each create their own counter, they can both issue ticket 1. Sharing one object is necessary for this requirement; global access is a separate design choice.

before.title: What Singleton adds, and what it combines
paragraphs: The Singleton pattern controls construction so callers reach one instance through a shared access operation. TicketDispenser has a private constructor and destructor, deleted copy operations, and a static instance function returning a reference. Ordinary callers cannot create another object or copy the existing one. The function returns a reference because it lends the service; callers must not delete it.

Singleton combines two ideas: restricting instance count and providing global access. You may need the first without needing the second. Passing one ordinary object from main often expresses sharing more clearly, because function parameters reveal who depends on the service. We implement Singleton here to understand its exact mechanism and costs, then use the lab to remove hidden access from a consumer.

static on instance means the member function is called on the class rather than on an existing object. There is no this pointer for that call. The local static variable inside it has a different meaning: its storage lasts beyond one function call. It is initialized when execution first reaches its declaration and is reused on later calls. The returned references therefore all name the same completed dispenser in this program.

before.title: Once-only initialization is not method synchronization
paragraphs: Since C++11, initialization of a function-local static is guarded so concurrent first callers do not each construct the object. One performs initialization while other callers wait for it to complete. If initialization throws, a later call can try again. Re-entering that same local static initialization recursively is not a safe way to resolve dependencies; avoid service constructors that cycle back through one another.

That guarantee concerns construction only. It does not protect later reads and writes to next_. Two threads incrementing an ordinary shared int without synchronization cause a data race and undefined behavior. It is not accurate to promise merely “one lost ticket”: the C++ program has no defined result for that race. Making the constructor private or the object global does not repair it.

The take operation uses a mutex, a lock that allows only one participating thread at a time into the protected region. lock_guard acquires gate_ when the guard is constructed and releases it when the guard leaves scope. Both the exhaustion check and the increment occur under that same lock. If the exception is thrown, stack cleanup still releases the lock. The local static guard and this method lock solve different problems and neither replaces the other.

The expression next_++ returns the old value and then increments the stored integer. The first three successful calls return 1, 2, and 3, leaving next_ equal to 4. Later calls test next_ > 3 and throw before incrementing again. The bounded sequence avoids overflow. Each whole take operation appears indivisible to other calls that use the same mutex. The standard does not promise fairness or which waiting caller gets a particular number.

before.title: Lifetime and tests reveal the hidden coupling
paragraphs: The instance is destroyed during normal program shutdown if it was successfully initialized. Its private destructor prevents ordinary callers from explicitly destroying the borrowed object. In this single executable the accessor identifies one service. Separate processes have separate address spaces and separate instances; dynamic-library boundaries can also require careful linkage and deployment rules. Singleton is not a machine-wide lock, a distributed coordinator, or a persistence mechanism.

Shutdown dependencies deserve care. Another static object’s destructor must not use a service whose lifetime has already ended. A main-owned service with explicit lifetime often makes this ordering easier to see. Deliberately leaking a service to avoid shutdown ordering changes resource cleanup behavior and should never be an unexamined default.

Tests in one process share singleton state. A test that consumes ticket 1 changes what another test sees. Running the second test alone may pass while running the whole suite fails. A reset-for-tests method can hide the problem and may create races if used while work is active. This chapter’s main is a fresh-process demonstration with a known initial state. Its sequential checks verify identity, numbering, and repeated exhaustion; they are not a concurrency stress test.

The lab introduces TicketSource as the operation a consumer needs. admit accepts TicketSource& rather than finding the singleton itself. The production boundary can pass TicketDispenser::instance(), while each test can create a fresh LocalTickets. That technique is dependency injection: supplying a needed object explicitly. It preserves the option of one production instance while making tests independent.

before.title: Choosing a shared service deliberately
paragraphs: A singleton can suit a truly process-wide service with a clear lifetime and little need for alternate instances. It is a poor fit when the program may run two independent sessions, load different configurations in tests, or need controlled startup and shutdown. Global access can make dependencies look smaller than they are because every function can silently acquire the service.

Do not replace every injected reference with a global accessor just to shorten parameter lists. Those parameters explain what the operation needs. Likewise, do not introduce an interface for every tiny value. TicketSource is justified in the lab by a concrete testing requirement: a consumer should work with independent counters as well as the shared production service.

For concurrency, one mutex protects only the state consistently accessed under it. If a future peek method reads next_ without locking, take’s lock does not make that new read safe. If two operations must form one transaction, locking each separately may still allow interleaving between them. Define the operation boundary first, then choose locking or an atomic design that preserves that boundary. Singleton answers where the object comes from; it does not answer every question about its correct use.

before.title: Pattern overview
paragraphs: Make an already useful object usable through the interface a caller already requires. The attached EPUB motivates this with incompatible data formats and a square peg presented as a round peg. Both problems demand a translator at the boundary. Learning Adapter means recognizing that mismatch before choosing inheritance or a wrapper.

The client calls the target operation. An adapter satisfies that target contract, calls the existing service through its different interface, and translates the result. In the normal attached C++ variant, Adapter inherits Target and stores an Adaptee pointer. before.title: The problem: one program, two meanings of weight
paragraphs: A parcel station decides whether a sample weighs at most two grams. Its application already asks a Scale for grams. A replacement device is not available. The old device returns an integer count of milligrams through milligrams(), and a negative value means the device failed. We must reuse that device without teaching every parcel rule its old spelling, units, and error convention. The answer must preserve fractions: 1,250 milligrams means 1.25 grams.

For one caller, the simplest reasonable answer is a direct conversion. Read the integer, reject negative results, and divide by 1000.0. A helper function could keep that operation in one place. If every caller can use that helper, stop there. A class does not improve a problem that is already solved clearly. Our added constraint is different: existing rules accept a Scale reference and may receive several kinds of scales at run time.

before.title: The failure that calls for a translator
paragraphs: Passing LegacyScale straight to light_enough does not compile. It is not a Scale, and it has no grams member. Merely renaming milligrams would still leave the wrong unit and would treat a failure signal as a very light parcel. Changing every rule would mix device concerns with parcel rules. Each new device would repeat that work.

An adapter is an object that makes an existing service meet another interface. An interface is the set of operations and promises callers may use. ScaleAdapter meets Scale by implementing grams. Inside that method it calls the old device, checks its result, and translates the unit. The caller sees grams throughout. The old device does not know that an adapter exists. This is useful at a boundary where two independently developed pieces already disagree.

before.title: What the C++ mechanism does
paragraphs: The colon in class ScaleAdapter final : public Scale declares public inheritance: the adapter may be used wherever a Scale is required. This is a type relationship, not a statement that the adapter owns a Scale object. The inherited pure virtual function, marked = 0 in Scale, demands an implementation. The override word asks the compiler to check that grams matches it, including its final const. A misspelled name or missing const produces a compile error instead of a hidden new method. final prevents further derivation; this example does not need another layer of subclasses.

At compilation, the compiler checks that light_enough may call grams through const Scale&. At execution, virtual dispatch selects ScaleAdapter::grams for our actual object. The ampersand makes scale a reference, so the function borrows the existing object rather than copying it. const prevents that call from modifying the object through this interface. It does not prove the physical sensor never changes. Here the simulated device stores one fixed reading, making our printed results repeatable.

ScaleAdapter also contains a reference, device_. Its constructor stores a connection to a LegacyScale that already exists. No device copy is made; no allocation is needed. The caller must keep that device alive for every adapter call. main creates device first and scale second. Local objects are destroyed in reverse order, so the adapter goes away before the device. Destroying the adapter does not destroy the borrowed device. Scale has a virtual destructor so a future owner holding a base-class pointer can destroy a derived adapter correctly.
