before.title: Units and errors are part of the contract
paragraphs: A boundary must translate meanings, not just names. In grams(), raw is checked before conversion. The value -1 is an error marker, not negative physical weight. Throwing std::runtime_error ends the normal call, so light_enough cannot accidentally accept the parcel. The error reaches the test's matching catch block. The adapter leaves both itself and its device unchanged when the call fails.

Dividing two integers discards the fractional part. Writing 1000.0 makes the divisor a double; the integer is converted for floating-point division. The returned double represents grams. This does not make floating-point arithmetic exact for every fraction. The test therefore uses a small tolerance when checking 1.25. The exact boundary values used here, two and zero, are represented exactly. A measurement system with strict legal or scientific rounding rules would need an explicit rule and perhaps an integer base unit throughout.

The contract assumes nonnegative integer milligrams are valid readings and all negatives signal failure. Real devices may distinguish timeout, overload, and calibration errors. An adapter should preserve distinctions the application needs instead of flattening every failure into zero. It should also avoid inventing precision: dividing an integer milligram count does not create a more precise measurement.

before.title: Composition and multiple inheritance
paragraphs: C++ also permits a class to inherit from two bases. A class adapter could inherit from Scale and LegacyScale, then use the inherited milligrams member. That approach may fit a legacy class designed for derivation, especially when overriding its virtual behavior is necessary. However, the adapter then contains its own legacy base subobject. It cannot automatically wrap the device instance that the application already owns. Public inheritance from the legacy type can also expose operations the new interface was meant to hide.

Our object adapter uses composition in the broad design sense of holding a connection to another object. The connection is borrowing, so the diagram uses a dependency arrow rather than an ownership diamond. It keeps lifetime policy with main and permits several adapters to view one device when that is intended. If the adapter should control the device's lifetime, a value member or unique_ptr would state a different ownership rule. Choose that rule from the actual device lifecycle, not from the pattern's name.

When debugging an adapter, write down three things before changing code: the input unit and error range, the target unit and error contract, and the lifetime owner. A wrong answer can come from any of them. When replacing a device library, keep the parcel tests unchanged and add device-specific adapter tests. That small boundary limits how far vendor changes travel through the program.

before.title: Two useful reports, two useful formats
paragraphs: A small inspection tool prints a count and also classifies that count. One screen wants count=6. Another wants [count:6]. The classification report calls counts above five high and all others normal. It must work in either format. Negative counts are invalid. Requirements now vary in two directions: what the report means, and how its fields are written.

The simplest first version returns a string directly from a function. That is a good solution when there is one meaning and one format. A second function can serve a second fixed report. The difficulty appears when both dimensions grow. If each combination has its own class, two report types and two formats need four combinations. Three types and four formats need twelve. The count is the product of the choices, not automatically an exponential function of one choice. What hurts is repeated policy and repeated formatting.

paragraphs: Suppose the warning boundary changes from five to ten. In the combined design, each warning-format class must change. Suppose the bracket screen changes its separator. A bridge is a stable connection between a high-level operation and a lower-level implementation that can vary independently. Here Report supplies the high-level render operation and borrows a Writer. before.title: Trace data and control across the bridge
paragraphs: In main, plain and brackets are created before the report objects that borrow them. cp stores a reference to plain; cb stores a reference to brackets. Calling cb.render(6) enters CountReport. validate first rejects a negative value. The report then sends the label count and integer 6 to writer_.field. Virtual dispatch selects Brackets::field. It creates [count:6] and returns that string by value through the report to main.

WarningReport follows the same route but chooses its label first. The conditional expression n > 5 ? "high" : "normal" evaluates the condition, selects exactly one of the two strings, and initializes label. The question mark introduces the true result, and the colon separates it from the false result. This colon is different from the colon that begins a constructor initializer list or a range loop. Syntax takes its meaning from its surrounding statement.

The returned strings own their character storage. The label passed to field is a const reference, so field borrows the argument during the call. Neither writer keeps that reference afterward. writer_ is a longer-lived borrow stored inside Report. Those are different lifetime obligations: a call parameter need only stay valid for the call, while a stored reference must stay valid for later calls too.

paragraphs: In main, plain and brackets are created before the report objects that borrow them. cp stores a reference to plain; cb stores a reference to brackets. Calling cb.render(6) enters CountReport. validate first rejects a negative value. The report then sends the label count and integer 6 to writer_.field. Virtual dispatch selects Brackets::field. It creates [count:6] and returns that string by value through the report to main.

WarningReport follows the same route but chooses its label first. The conditional expression n > 5 ? "high" : "normal" evaluates the condition, selects exactly one of the two strings, and initializes label. The question mark introduces the true result, and the colon separates it from the false result. This colon is different from the colon that begins a constructor initializer list or a range loop. Syntax takes its meaning from its surrounding statement.

The returned strings own their character storage. The label passed to field is a const reference, so field borrows the argument during the call. Neither writer keeps that reference afterward. writer_ is a longer-lived borrow stored inside Report. Those are different lifetime obligations: a call parameter need only stay valid for the call, while a stored reference must stay valid for later calls too.

before.title: What compilation guarantees and what it cannot
paragraphs: The compiler checks public inheritance, virtual signatures, and whether each concrete class implements the required operation. override catches a mismatch. protected makes writer_ and validate available to the derived reports while keeping them out of ordinary client code. The helper is static because it depends only on its argument and needs no Report object. Constructors initialize the reference before any render call can occur.

The compiler does not verify that a new Writer preserves the label and value faithfully. A writer could accidentally swap field names or drop a minus sign. That would still compile. The shared semantic contract is therefore essential: format the supplied name and integer without changing their meaning. The report checks the domain rule that counts cannot be negative. The generic writer is capable of formatting any integer, which makes it usable in other domains.

At execution the same report can use either writer selected during construction. Our design does not provide a setter to switch writer_ later; C++ references cannot be rebound. To change format, construct a new report borrowing another writer. This keeps ownership and configuration simple. An application needing live format changes could instead hold a non-owning pointer with an explicit non-null rule or own an interchangeable writer. That requirement has not appeared here, so its extra states are unnecessary.

before.title: When the split helps, and when it does not
paragraphs: A bridge gives independence only when the interface is stable and truthful. If field lacks data one format needs, reports may begin checking for special writers. That is a warning that the boundary is too narrow or the supposedly independent dimensions are actually linked. Improve the contract using a real use case, or accept a smaller set of supported combinations. Do not promise that every conceivable report will work with every renderer.

An enum and one formatting function may be smaller when the set of formats is fixed and tiny. A template can select a writer at compilation and may remove virtual calls, but it exposes more implementation to callers and moves the choice from runtime to build time. Neither alternative is inherently inferior. The reason for this bridge is the already demonstrated independent growth in report policy and presentation.

Bridge and Adapter can produce similar shapes in a diagram. Their motivations differ. An adapter repairs an existing disagreement between interfaces. A bridge deliberately separates dimensions that should evolve independently. When reviewing a change, ask what boundary is being protected. Add tests for each report's meaning and each format's text, plus a few combinations. That protects the separation more effectively than checking only class names.

before.question: What is Composite?
before.answer: A design in which leaves and containers support the same useful operation over a tree.

before.question: What is Leaf?
before.answer: A tree node with no children.

before.question: What is Recursion?
before.answer: Solving a problem by calling the same operation on smaller parts until a stopping case is reached.

before.question: What is Acyclic?
before.answer: Having no path that leads back to an earlier node.

before.question: Is Group still a Composite without Add, Remove, or IsComposite on Work?
before.answer: Yes. Group implements Work and recursively queries Work children. Runtime editing and discovery are optional interface choices.

before.question: Would copying the attached parent_ pointer into an owning smart pointer be safe?
before.answer: No. The parent already owns downward in our tree. A strong owner back upward risks ownership cycles or double ownership; the parent link must be non-owning and kept consistent.

before.title: A flat list works until a task contains tasks
paragraphs: A work plan contains steps measured in minutes. A step lasts from zero to ten thousand minutes. A group may contain steps and smaller groups. The tool must report the total for either a single step or an entire project. An empty group totals zero. A result above ten thousand minutes is rejected rather than silently accepted. This upper bound is a business rule and also makes integer arithmetic easy to reason about.

For a flat list, start with a vector of integers and a loop that adds them. Nothing about that problem requires a class family. The limitation arrives when groups can contain groups. Keeping one vector for steps and another for groups forces each caller to understand both types and every nesting level. A hard-coded loop for two levels fails as soon as a third group appears. We need one operation whose meaning stays valid at any depth.

before.title: One operation for a part and a whole
paragraphs: Composite is a design for a tree whose individual items and containers support the same useful operation. A tree is a structure with one root and child branches, where following child links never leads back to an ancestor. A leaf has no children. In this example Step is a leaf, Group is a container, and Work is their shared contract. Work::minutes asks for total work time without asking which kind of object receives the request.

Step returns its stored duration. Group asks each child for its minutes and adds the answers. A child group repeats that process. This repeated call on a smaller part of the same problem is recursion. Recursion stops at a Step or an empty Group, so each valid finite tree eventually returns a result. A caller needs only one expression, work.minutes(), whether it measures one step or a project containing many groups.

The contract deliberately does not put add or remove on Work. Adding a child makes sense for a container but not for a leaf. Pretending every leaf can accept a child would create confusing no-op methods or runtime errors. Our groups receive their full child lists during construction and then expose only the query. That is enough for the current requirement and keeps the assembled topology stable.

before.title: Build ownership from the leaves upward
paragraphs: Children is a type alias for a vector of unique_ptr<Work>. The vector owns its pointer objects, and each unique_ptr owns exactly one Work object. The virtual destructor in Work ensures that deleting through the base type destroys a complete Step or Group. When a group is destroyed, its vector destroys its children. Child groups then destroy their own children. The project owns the complete tree through a chain of clearly stated owners.

main first creates two Step objects for ten and twenty minutes. It moves their vector into a Group, then moves that child group into another vector alongside a five-minute Step. Finally it moves that vector into project. std::move permits ownership transfer; it does not copy the work objects. The source vector remains valid after its move, but the program does not depend on its size or contents. Its old children are now owned through the new container.

Group rejects a null child in its constructor. If validation throws, already-constructed member objects are destroyed automatically, including their owned children. No manual delete loop is needed. Since the public API only builds groups from completed children and does not later attach an existing group beneath a descendant, ordinary bottom-up construction yields an acyclic tree. This does not excuse creating a unique_ptr from an already-owned raw pointer; that would violate ownership rules before this API could protect the program.

before.title: Follow the return values, not just the arrows
paragraphs: For the supplied project, the outer Group starts total at zero. Its first child is another Group. That inner group receives ten from its first leaf and twenty from its second, then returns thirty. The outer group adds thirty and next receives five. It returns thirty-five. Each group has its own local total. The locals exist in separate function calls, so the inner subtotal does not overwrite the outer subtotal.

In for (const auto& child : children_), the colon means take each element from children_ in sequence. child is a const reference to a unique_ptr already in the vector. It is not a copy; unique ownership must not be copied. The arrow in child->minutes() follows the pointer to the owned Work object and calls its virtual function. const on minutes says the operation does not change the tree through that interface. Every invocation computes fresh local state instead of storing a running total in a member.

Before adding n, Group checks whether n is greater than 10000 - total. If so, it throws overflow_error. Despite the exception name, the rejected condition here is the project's allowed budget, reached well before the built-in int limit. Testing before addition avoids doing an unsafe addition and only checking after damage. The nonnegative child contract makes the subtraction and comparison meaningful. A future Work implementation that returns negative minutes would break that contract even if its code compiled.

before.title: Cost, depth, and the limits of uniform operations
paragraphs: The compiler checks that Step and Group provide minutes, and that an owning vector cannot be copied accidentally. At execution, virtual dispatch selects the correct child operation at each link. A complete query visits every node once, so its work grows in proportion to the number of nodes. Recursive calls use stack space proportional to tree depth. A million siblings and a million nested groups pose different risks: the latter may exhaust the call stack.

For an untrusted input format, enforce a depth limit while parsing or use an explicit stack for traversal. Our small, internally assembled tree has no parser and no arbitrary-depth guarantee. Caching a group total could make repeated reads cheaper, but would add invalidation concerns if editing later becomes possible. Since this tree is fixed after construction, storing a checked total at construction could also be reasonable when queries dominate. The example recomputes totals so the recursive mechanism stays visible.

Composite fits operations that make sense on both a part and a whole. A total duration qualifies. A command such as set_leaf_duration does not naturally apply to every container. Keep type-specific editing outside the uniform query contract. When maintaining the system, add a new leaf only after defining how it contributes to totals, ownership, and failure behavior. A new class name alone does not make a safe new component.

before.title: Pattern overview
paragraphs: Add optional behavior around an individual object without writing one subclass for every feature combination. The attached EPUB uses layered notifications and a data source with encoding and compression. The important requirement is that a wrapper remains usable through the component interface, so another wrapper can be placed around it.

Component defines the shared operation. A concrete component supplies the basic result. Each decorator implements that same contract and stores another Component connection. Calls travel inward through the wrapper chain; returned results travel outward and can be changed at each layer. The client chooses the order of the layers. Different orders may have different meanings, even when the component and wrapper types are identical.

before.title: When two small features produce many variants
paragraphs: A status panel starts with plain text such as ready now. Some screens add WARN before the text. Some limit the display to five characters. A screen may need both behaviors, and its policy must say which applies first. For this chapter, strings contain simple single-byte characters. The program is not a full Unicode layout engine.

With one fixed policy, a direct expression is the simplest implementation. Add the prefix and take a substring. That clearly states the order. The problem appears when screens choose different combinations at runtime. Classes named PrefixedMessage, LimitedMessage, PrefixedLimitedMessage, and LimitedPrefixedMessage repeat pieces of behavior. Adding a suffix or a timestamp creates more combinations. We need reusable features that can be assembled without defining a new class for every pairing.

discussion.question: Why can adding a prefix before trimming text differ from adding it after trimming?
discussion.answer: Trimming the prefixed result can remove part of the original message or suffix. Trimming the original first leaves the later prefix outside the limit. Order is part of the requirement, not an implementation detail.

before.title: A wrapper with the same public operation
paragraphs: A decorator is an object that adds behavior around another object while keeping the same interface. Message provides text(). Plain returns its stored text. Prefix and Limit are also Messages, but each owns an inner Message and calls that object's text before adding its own behavior. Since the inner object may itself be another decorator, the same construction rule supports a chain of features.

The important fact is that every layer remains usable as a Message. This is why the common interface is needed now: callers must accept an assembled chain without knowing its exact shape. Public inheritance supplies that substitutability. Containing an inner Message supplies the behavior being extended. The inheritance link and the ownership link answer different questions and must remain distinct in the diagram.

We do not add a generic Decorator base class merely to repeat the inner_ member. Two small wrappers do not yet need that additional inheritance layer. If many wrappers later share forwarding behavior and validation, a base wrapper can remove useful duplication. First show the repeated need; then judge whether sharing that implementation makes the code easier to change.

before.title: Order is visible behavior
paragraphs: The first chain is Prefix around Limit around Plain. A call enters Prefix, which asks Limit for text. Limit asks Plain and receives ready now. Limit keeps the first five characters, ready, and returns them. Prefix then adds WARN and returns WARN ready. The five-character rule applied only to the inner body, so the final string is longer than five.

The second chain is Limit around Prefix around Plain. Plain again returns ready now. Prefix returns WARN ready now. The outer Limit keeps its first five characters: W, A, R, N, and a space. The printed single quotes make the trailing space visible. The final result is 'WARN '. This is not an implementation accident. The outermost operation runs last on the returned text in this design.

Operations whose order changes the result are noncommutative: swapping them changes behavior. Prefix and Limit are a concrete example. Never document a stack merely as 'prefix plus limit' if the order matters. Show the nesting or the actual transformation sequence. For logging, validation, caching, and compression wrappers in real systems, a wrong order can matter much more than a shortened message.

before.title: Follow ownership separately from the call stack
paragraphs: Each wrapper stores unique_ptr<Message>. Its constructor receives an owner by value and moves that owner into inner_. The caller gives up ownership as part of construction. A null pointer is rejected immediately, so text can safely call inner_->text without a null check on every request. If construction throws, the already-initialized member owner cleans up its inner object automatically.

make_unique constructs each object and returns its owner. main nests those calls from the plain object outward. When first is destroyed, its Prefix is destroyed, which destroys its inner Limit, which destroys its Plain. Message has a virtual destructor so deleting through unique_ptr<Message> reaches the correct derived destructor. No caller needs to remember the chain's exact concrete types to clean it up.

During text(), each layer also creates local strings. body receives the inner result by value; result stores this layer's transformed text. These values own their character storage, so the method never returns a reference to a local string. Returning a string value permits safe transfer of the result to the caller. The chain's object lifetime is much longer than each local string's lifetime, and the two should not be confused.

Message explicitly allows default construction but deletes copy and move construction and assignment. The = delete notation asks the compiler to reject those operations. Derived wrappers therefore cannot be moved as whole objects, which would empty inner_ in the source and violate its non-null rule. Move the owning unique_ptr handle instead: ownership changes hands while the wrapper object and its inner chain stay in place. Compile-time static_assert checks use the type traits from <type_traits> to verify that Prefix and Limit cannot be copied or moved. The Suffix solution checks the same property. A type trait is a library query about a type; static_assert rejects a false condition during compilation.

before.title: Syntax, cost, and boundary assumptions
paragraphs: The compiler verifies that every concrete Message implements text() const with the right return type. override makes the check explicit. const permits reading through a const Message reference and promises not to alter the object through that method's ordinary members. It does not automatically make an arbitrary chain thread-safe if future decorators introduce mutable caches or shared services.

At execution, virtual dispatch chooses each layer and each layer delegates once. substr(0, limit_) begins at position zero and takes at most limit_ characters. If the requested length is larger than the body, it returns the whole body. A zero limit returns an empty string. std::size_t is an unsigned size type; a negative signed value converted to it would become a large positive size. The program constructs limits from nonnegative literals, and a user-input interface would need to reject negative values before conversion.

A chain with many layers may allocate and copy many intermediate strings. This example favors clarity over a claim of best performance. A fixed transformation pipeline made of ordinary functions can be simpler and cheaper when callers do not need objects sharing an interface. A streaming design may avoid large intermediates, but then each layer must define how it handles partial input and failures.

Decorator is useful when features are independently selectable and have a consistent component contract. It is less useful when the features depend on many details of one another or when an object needs a radically different interface. Keep the assembly code readable, test the important orders, and document whether repeated decoration is meaningful. Applying Prefix twice adds two prefixes; it is not automatically idempotent, meaning it does not necessarily leave the result unchanged after the first application.

before.title: Pattern overview
paragraphs: Provide one convenient operation for a task that otherwise requires knowledge of several subsystem objects and their call order. The attached EPUB motivates a complicated conversion library. A Facade gives ordinary callers a smaller entrance to useful work; it does not require removing the lower-level interfaces or pretending the whole subsystem has become simple internally.

The client calls a task-level method on Facade. Facade knows which subsystem methods to call, which results to pass onward, and which order to preserve. Subsystem classes continue doing their own jobs without knowing about the facade. This pattern does not require a base class or virtual function: delegation and a simpler public task contract are the central mechanism.

before.title: A small request with several hidden steps
paragraphs: An inspection screen accepts whitespace-separated integer readings and displays their count and total. Each reading must be between -100 and 100. There must be at least one reading and at most one thousand. Tokens such as 4x and 1.5 are invalid. The screen should ask for a summary, not repeat parsing rules and subsystem call order in every event handler.

The simplest implementation for one screen is a direct sequence: parse text, validate the vector, then summarize it. That is a reasonable function, and the pattern does not require making it a class. Trouble begins when several screens repeat the sequence. One may forget validation. Another may summarize first, so invalid data reaches arithmetic. A third may accept a valid prefix of a malformed token. The application's simple request has become tied to the details of three services.

before.title: A small doorway rather than a new object hierarchy
paragraphs: A facade is a simpler public entrance to a set of related operations. Importer::run accepts text and returns Stats. Internally it performs the required steps in the required order. It does not introduce inheritance because no interchangeable family of importers is needed. Parser, Validator, and Summarizer are ordinary member objects. Their lifetimes are part of Importer itself.

The facade gives a name to a useful application operation: import readings and produce a valid summary. It does not merely rename every subsystem method. A facade with parse, validate, summarize, configure_parser, configure_validator, and many other forwarded operations would force everyday callers to understand the old sequencing problem again. Advanced callers can still use the smaller subsystem types directly when they accept those responsibilities.

The component classes here make the boundary visible in a complete small program. In a tiny project, these could be free functions and run could be the facade function. The reason to keep the boundary is consistency of use; the decision to store member objects is separate. A larger subsystem might keep parser options or other state in these members, but this example does not invent state just to justify classes.

before.title: Parsing must consume the whole token
paragraphs: Parser first uses istringstream to split on whitespace. The extraction expression input >> token succeeds when it obtains another string token. The while loop continues only on success. An empty or whitespace-only input therefore returns an empty vector; deciding whether that count is acceptable belongs to Validator.

For each token, std::from_chars tries to read a base-ten integer into n. Its result contains an error code, ec, and a pointer, ptr, marking where parsing stopped. Success requires both no error and ptr equal to the token's end. Parsing 4x can read the integer 4 successfully but stops at x, so the second condition rejects it. Parsing an integer outside the representable int range sets an error. The code never uses n unless both checks pass.

The end pointer is token.data() plus token.size(): the position just after the final character. That position is valid for comparison and as an end marker, but it is not a character the parser should dereference. data supplies contiguous character storage, and from_chars borrows it only during the call. Parser stores the integer value in its vector, not a pointer into token. Reusing token on the next loop iteration is therefore safe.

This narrow grammar accepts a leading minus sign and ordinary decimal digits. Integer from_chars does not accept a leading plus sign. Whitespace is handled outside it by the stream. The contract intentionally does not accept decimal fractions, thousands separators, or locale-specific numbers. If those become requirements, update the grammar and tests explicitly instead of hoping a different conversion function happens to accept them.

before.title: Validation establishes arithmetic assumptions
paragraphs: Validator checks count before checking each value. The count must be in the closed range one through one thousand, and each value must be in the closed range -100 through 100. Closed means both endpoints are allowed. With those limits, a total lies between -100000 and 100000. That is well within int on the supported compiler environment, which uses at least 32-bit int for these examples.

Summarizer relies on that validated-input precondition. A precondition is a rule the caller must make true before calling an operation. Its local total begins at zero and adds each value exactly once. Stats stores the number of values as std::size_t and the total as int. The brace return {v.size(), total} initializes these members in their declared order. It does not attach references to the input vector.

Importer enforces the precondition by calling validate before summarize. If parsing or validation throws, control leaves run immediately; calculation is skipped and no Stats value is returned. The input string remains unchanged. The local vector is destroyed when the function exits normally or because of an exception. Because this example has no external writes, failure cannot leave a half-written file or partially updated database.

This is not an automatic transaction mechanism. A facade that writes to two files can still fail after writing the first. Such a workflow needs a separate recovery or commit design. A simple public method reduces caller complexity; it does not erase the failure modes of the operations it coordinates.

before.title: Compilation, performance, and a maintainable boundary
paragraphs: All calls in this example are direct calls to concrete types. The compiler checks signatures and may inline small methods. No virtual dispatch or heap-based object hierarchy is needed. The vector may allocate while collecting input, and strings and streams manage their own storage. At execution, values move from text tokens to integers to a checked summary. Control follows the three-stage sequence shown in the diagram.

The one-thousand count check protects the calculation, but parsing still builds the vector before validation. This is acceptable for the bounded local example and is not a denial-of-service defense for unlimited network input. A production ingestion service should stop reading after its token or byte limit, before allocating for the entire request. That change belongs at the input boundary and needs tests of the chosen maximum.

When replacing a parser, keep the facade's accepted grammar and rejected cases stable unless a requirement changes. When adding a new summary, decide whether it belongs in Stats or deserves another operation. Avoid turning Importer into a giant class that manages screens, persistence, authentication, and printing. A useful facade has one coherent purpose. Separate facades can expose other workflows over the same subsystem without making every client know every service.

The key debugging question is where a guarantee is established. Parser establishes valid integer syntax. Validator establishes domain and count bounds. Summarizer assumes those bounds. Importer connects them. If an invalid value reaches arithmetic, inspect the call order and the bypass paths rather than adding random checks to the output screen.

before.title: Repeated data can outweigh useful differences
paragraphs: A drawing tool places many marks on a page. A mark has a style name, a style size, and a horizontal position. Thousands of marks may use the same style while each position differs. For a few marks, store all three fields directly in every object. That is simple, clear, and often the right answer.

The limitation appears when the shared portion becomes large. Imagine that a style later contains a loaded shape outline or a rendering table. Copying that payload for every mark may consume far more memory than the positions themselves. Before changing the design, measure the repeated data and the number of uses. Our small program keeps style data intentionally short so the ownership mechanism is visible; it is not evidence that this tiny representation saves memory.

before.title: Split stable shared data from each use
paragraphs: Flyweight is a memory-sharing design that stores repeated state once and gives each use a connection to it. The shared state is called intrinsic state. Here name and size identify the style. The state that belongs to a particular use is called extrinsic state. Here x is the mark's position. A Mark holds a shared style owner and its own x value. Two Marks can therefore agree on style without becoming the same mark.

StylePool looks up a style by a Key containing both name and size. If that key already exists, it returns another shared owner of the same Style object. Otherwise it creates one immutable Style, stores an owner in the map, and returns another owner. Reusing an existing object is often called interning. It is useful only when equality of the chosen key truly means the shared data is interchangeable.

The key is a std::pair<std::string, int>, not two fields joined into an unstructured string. A pair keeps field boundaries unambiguous. If a later style includes color, color must become part of the key too. A pool keyed only by name would wrongly reuse dot size twelve for a request for dot size twenty. The visible mistake would be a correct position with the wrong style size.

before.title: Read the shared pointer type carefully
paragraphs: StylePtr is an alias for std::shared_ptr<const Style>. shared_ptr means several owners can keep the same object alive. const Style means the object reached through this owner is read-only. It is not the same as const shared_ptr<Style>, which would prevent reseating that particular pointer variable but would still permit changing the Style through it.

The pool constructs the object with make_shared<const Style>. The actual allocated Style is const, not merely viewed through one const handle while another mutable handle is retained. Its fields are initialized once and then read. Immutability means the object does not change after construction. That matters because a mutation to one shared style could otherwise change every mark using it. The public fields remain safe to read because access is through a pointer to const; the pool gives out no mutable owner.

A shared_ptr copy increments a shared ownership count; it does not copy the Style. When one pointer is destroyed, the count decreases. The object remains alive while at least one owner remains. The pool owns styles through its map, and each Mark owns its style through style_. This is shared ownership, so an ownership diagram must not imply that a mark exclusively owns its style. paragraphs: StylePtr is an alias for std::shared_ptr<const Style>. shared_ptr means several owners can keep the same object alive. const Style means the object reached through this owner is read-only. It is not the same as const shared_ptr<Style>, which would prevent reseating that particular pointer variable but would still permit changing the Style through it.

The pool constructs the object with make_shared<const Style>. The actual allocated Style is const, not merely viewed through one const handle while another mutable handle is retained. Its fields are initialized once and then read. Immutability means the object does not change after construction. That matters because a mutation to one shared style could otherwise change every mark using it. The public fields remain safe to read because access is through a pointer to const; the pool gives out no mutable owner.

paragraphs: main requests (dot,12) twice. The first lookup misses, creates one Style, and stores it. The second lookup finds the existing entry and returns found->second, which is the map's shared_ptr value. first and same therefore point to the same object. Mark left takes an owner of the twelve-size style and stores x = 3. Mark right receives another owner of that same style and stores x = 8. draw reads the shared name and size, then appends its own position. The outputs dot/12@3 and dot/12@8 show the separation directly. Neither draw call changes the style or the other mark.

In draw, const auto& name borrows the string inside Style while the Mark's owner keeps the Style alive. const auto size copies the small integer. Both are suitable choices: copying an int is cheap; copying the string is unnecessary for this local read. The returned formatted string is a new owned value. before.title: Lifetime is independent of the pool scope
paragraphs: The program creates a short-lived StylePool inside a nested scope and saves one returned owner in survivor outside that scope. When the pool is destroyed, its map releases its owner. survivor still owns the Style, so reading survivor->name afterward is valid. This test checks a real advantage of shared ownership: the pool's lifetime need not enclose every use.

The pool uses strong owners, so it also retains each style until the pool is destroyed or entries are removed. An unused style does not vanish merely because its last Mark disappears. That is a cache-retention policy, not a leak caused by missing delete. A long-running application may require a size limit, explicit clearing, or weak_ptr entries. A weak pointer observes a shared object without keeping it alive, but it requires checking whether the object still exists before reuse. That complexity should be justified by actual retention needs.

The compiler checks const access and pointer types; it cannot prove that the key includes every meaningful field. At runtime, map lookup compares keys and finds a matching entry. std::map lookup takes logarithmic comparisons in the number of styles. shared_ptr adds a control block and ownership bookkeeping. Neither cost disappears because the design has a name.

before.title: Calculate the tradeoff before calling it an optimization
paragraphs: Suppose N marks each have U bytes of unique state and would otherwise carry S bytes of shared payload. The direct representation costs roughly N times (U + S), ignoring container and allocation overhead. With K distinct styles and a per-mark handle of H bytes, sharing costs roughly N times (U + H) plus K times S, plus pool and control-block overhead. When K is nearly N or S is tiny, sharing may lose. When S is large and K is much smaller than N, it can win substantially.

This example does not report exact saved bytes because object layout, string storage, allocator overhead, and platform details matter. Measure the real workload. Also test semantic isolation: changing a mark's position must not change another mark, and equal style keys should share exactly when that is part of the pool contract. Flyweight is a targeted optimization, not a reason to turn every small value into a shared pointer.

before.title: A cheap question can trigger expensive work
paragraphs: A visitor display asks for a building's opening hour. In a real system that answer may require opening a connection or reading a remote schedule. This example uses a tiny in-memory Source so the behavior is deterministic. The source hour starts at eight, and a reads counter records real-service requests. The interface accepts hours already supplied by a trusted source; it does not validate a full calendar or time zone.

The simplest caller invokes the real service every time. That is appropriate when the service is cheap and fresh data matters more than reuse. The new requirements are to avoid creating the real service until needed, reuse the most recently fetched hour until told it is stale, and deny reads when local permission has been revoked. Repeating those rules at every caller would spread state management and make it easy to return a cached value after access was removed.

before.title: Use the same interface with an access-controlling substitute
paragraphs: A proxy is a substitute object that controls access to another service while offering the same interface. Hours defines opening(). RealHours reads Source and increments its reads counter. HoursProxy also implements opening, but it checks permission, checks its cache, creates RealHours if necessary, and calls it only when a fresh value is needed. Code written against Hours can use either object.

The proxy holds a Source reference and an optional unique_ptr<RealHours>. The pointer starts empty. Constructing the proxy therefore does not construct RealHours. Creating the real object only on first demand is called lazy initialization. Once created, the real service remains owned by the proxy even if cached data is invalidated. The two states answer different questions: is a service object present, and is there a remembered result?

Caching means retaining a result for later reuse. std::optional<int> stores either no value or one integer. It is a better representation than using zero as an empty marker because midnight, hour zero, is valid. Testing cached_ asks whether a value exists; it does not ask whether the stored integer is nonzero. Dereferencing it with *cached_ reads that value only after the program knows it is present.

before.title: Permission comes before the fast path
paragraphs: opening first checks allowed_. If false, it throws runtime_error immediately. It does this before consulting cached_. Revoking permission must stop both real-service reads and returns of data fetched earlier. A misplaced permission check after the cache hit would deny new reads but still expose old cached data. That is a precise ordering bug, not a reason to abandon caching.

This Boolean permission is a local teaching model, not an authentication system. There is no user identity, secret, network enforcement, or protection against a caller directly using RealHours. In a real application, access decisions need an authoritative policy and a boundary that unauthorized callers cannot bypass. The pattern explains where a check can sit; it does not make the check trustworthy by itself.

After permission succeeds, an engaged cache returns immediately without creating or reading a real service. On a cache miss, the proxy creates RealHours only if real_ is still empty. Then it calls real_->opening, stores the returned integer in cached_, and returns it. The virtual interface is the same, but allowed caching deliberately changes freshness. That semantic difference must be part of the service contract a caller accepts.

before.title: Trace old data and explicit invalidation
paragraphs: The first opening call sees no cache and no real service. It creates RealHours, reads eight, stores eight, and leaves source.reads equal to one. main changes source.hour to nine. The next opening call still returns eight, and the read counter stays one. That stale value is expected under this cache policy. Stale means no longer known to match the current source.

invalidate calls cached_.reset(), which removes the stored result but leaves real_ alive. The next permitted opening call reuses the already-created service object, reads nine, stores it, and advances reads to two. main then denies access and confirms that even this warm cache cannot be read. After re-enabling access, it changes the source to zero, invalidates, and calls twice. Both calls return zero, but only the first reads the source, leaving the final counter at three.

An invalidation policy says when remembered data stops being usable. This program makes that decision explicit in main. It does not watch Source automatically. A production design might attach a revision number, receive a change notification, use a maximum age, or always fetch fresh data for critical operations. Each choice has a cost and a freshness promise. A cache without a stated invalidation policy is an unfinished design.

before.title: Object lifetime and failure state
paragraphs: main creates Source before HoursProxy, so the borrowed source outlives the proxy. The proxy owns its RealHours through unique_ptr. RealHours itself borrows the same Source. Destroying the proxy destroys the optional cache and the real-service owner, but it does not destroy Source. Local declaration order supplies the required lifetime arrangement without manual deletion.

At compilation, override checks that both classes implement Hours::opening. The method is not const because obtaining an answer may change the cache and the source's diagnostic counter. A logically read-only business operation can still mutate implementation state; the interface should state that honestly rather than adding mutable everywhere without discussing consequences.

If allocation of RealHours fails, the owner remains empty and the cache remains empty. If a future real-service call throws before returning an integer, assignment to cached_ is not reached, so a miss remains uncached. The example's real service does not throw, but placing assignment after a successful call naturally avoids remembering a fabricated success. The exact state of a real service after its own failure would still depend on that service's contract.

The program is single-threaded. Concurrent calls could race while creating real_, reading Source, or changing cached_. shared ownership or virtual functions would not fix those races. A concurrent version would need synchronization and a clear rule for the order of revocation, invalidation, and in-flight requests. We do not add those mechanisms without the requirement because they would obscure the state transitions being taught.

Hours defaults construction but explicitly deletes copy and move operations. The = delete declarations make service objects stable in place; callers transfer an owning unique_ptr handle when ownership must change. Without this rule, an implicit proxy move would transfer real_ while leaving copied scalar cache and permission state in the source, creating two surprising service identities. Preventing object moves keeps the lifecycle contract simpler. Static type-trait checks verify that HoursProxy is neither copy-constructible nor move-constructible.

If a future real-service call throws before returning an integer, assignment to cached_ is not reached, so a miss remains uncached. The example's real service does not throw, but placing assignment after a successful call naturally avoids remembering a fabricated success. The exact state of a real service after its own failure would still depend on that service's contract.

The program is single-threaded. Concurrent calls could race while creating real_, reading Source, or changing cached_. shared ownership or virtual functions would not fix those races. A concurrent version would need synchronization and a clear rule for the order of revocation, invalidation, and in-flight requests. We do not add those mechanisms without the requirement because they would obscure the state transitions being taught.

Hours defaults construction but explicitly deletes copy and move operations. The = delete declarations make service objects stable in place; callers transfer an owning unique_ptr handle when ownership must change. Without this rule, an implicit proxy move would transfer real_ while leaving copied scalar cache and permission state in the source, creating two surprising service identities. Preventing object moves keeps the lifecycle contract simpler. Static type-trait checks verify that HoursProxy is neither copy-constructible nor move-constructible.

paragraphs: Proxy and Decorator can both implement an interface and contain another implementation. A decorator normally adds independently selectable behavior to a component. A proxy stands in for a service to control access, location, or lifecycle. Our proxy creates its own real service on demand and manages a freshness policy. A diagram alone cannot settle which intent best describes a design; the requirements explain it.

For an inexpensive local value, directly reading Source may be simpler than either wrapper. For a service used exactly once, caching may add memory and complexity without avoiding work. Measure actual request patterns before optimizing. When a proxy is useful, expose enough diagnostics to test the behavior. The reads counter and loaded query let the example verify avoided work rather than merely checking that the printed hour looks right.

before.title: Pattern overview
paragraphs: Send a request through an ordered set of possible handlers without making its caller select the final receiver. Each handler decides whether this request belongs to it. This chapter teaches the first-handler-wins form shown by the attached C++ sample; the EPUB also explains a validation form in which several checks run until one stops the request.

The essential choice is handle or pass onward. The caller supplies the request and an entry point. A handler that declines allows the next handler to try. before.title: The problem: one job, one responsible desk
paragraphs: A small print workshop receives a Job containing a format name and a page count. Labels should go to a label desk; ordinary reports go to a general desk. The general desk can also print labels when the special desk is absent. Each job must reach at most one desk. The workshop rejects a page count below one or above one thousand before considering any desk. Unsupported formats must produce a visible unhandled result. No real printing happens in this teaching program: it chooses a destination so that routing can be checked without consuming supplies.

For two fixed destinations, an if statement is a sound start. Read the format, choose a destination, and return. There is no need to build a class family merely because several destinations exist. The limit appears when different workshop shifts need different ordered sets of rules. Copying the whole function for each shift also copies validation and fallback behavior. One shift may then accept zero-page jobs while another rejects them. We need to assemble the choices while keeping the routing contract in one place.

before.title: Make each choice a small, honest question
paragraphs: A handler is a piece of code that accepts a request, decides whether it can handle it, and reports that decision. A chain of responsibility is an ordered set of these handlers. The delivered program represents each handler as a function. Rule is a short name, introduced by using, for std::function<Reply(const Job&)>. This standard wrapper can hold different callable objects with the same call shape. Here the shape means: borrow a read-only Job and return a Reply. The program does not need a next pointer inside every handler because a vector already stores their order.

Reply is std::optional<std::string>: it contains either one destination string or no string. std::nullopt explicitly means there is no answer here. That is different from an answer whose string happens to be empty. The if (reply) condition asks whether a value exists. The expression *reply then accesses that value; the asterisk is safe because the presence check came first. A missing answer is ordinary control flow, not an exception. The caller receives a separate text result, unhandled, only after every handler declines.

before.title: Follow control and data through the chain
paragraphs: route first checks the page count. The test uses ||, meaning that either bad bound is enough to reject the job. Valid jobs enter a range-based for loop. In for (const auto& rule : rules), the colon means take each item from rules in order. auto obtains the function-wrapper type from the vector; the reference avoids copying that wrapper; const prevents this loop from changing it. The same read-only Job is borrowed by each call. No handler owns the job, stores its address, or extends its lifetime.

For a label job, label_rule returns a value, so route returns immediately. general_rule is never called for that request. For a report, the first handler returns no value and the second supplies the destination. For archive, both decline. The compiler checks that each stored callable has the required input and result shape. Which handler supplies the answer is decided during execution from the job and the order of rules. Moving the rules into a different vector can change behavior without recompiling route, although changing the source initializer still requires rebuilding the executable.

before.title: First-handler routing is not an all-stage pipeline
paragraphs: A pipeline is a sequence in which several stages may each perform part of the work. A document pipeline might validate pages, add a tracking code, write a record, and print. Success at one stage normally means continue. Our chain has a different rule: an answer means stop. If a maintainer converts return *reply into an assignment and continues looping, the general desk can replace the label desk because both accept labels. With real printing, that same mistake could produce two copies. The word chain alone does not tell a reader which stopping rule applies.

Decide the rule before choosing an interface. In a validation pipeline, an enum such as Continue or Reject makes sense; in this router, optional destination makes sense. Mixing both meanings in one bool makes it hard to tell whether true means finished or allowed to continue. Shared requirements such as a valid page count belong before routing. A handler that is optional in one configuration must not be the only place that enforces a mandatory check. The empty-rule test proves that having no handlers remains a defined situation.

before.title: Boundaries, costs, and a practical review
paragraphs: The handlers are pure selection functions: their result depends on the job, and they do not print, store files, or change outside data. This makes order tests cheap and repeatable. With n handlers, an unsupported request makes n calls; an early match needs fewer. std::function offers runtime flexibility but may allocate when storing a large callable. For this tiny fixed router, direct calls or a table of plain function pointers can cost less. Neither performance claim should replace a measurement if routing is on a busy path.

Before adding a rule in real software, inspect overlap, position, failure meaning, and ownership. A fallback placed first can hide every special case. A rule that captures a local reference and survives that local variable can later access a dead object. The current vector stores free functions, so it has no such captured lifetime. A linked chain would also need a no-cycle rule; this vector traversal has no link cycle to create. The model deliberately omits retries and external actions. Choosing a destination successfully does not prove that the destination later completed the job.

before.title: The problem: moving a marker is easy until timing changes
paragraphs: A planning screen shows a marker at an integer position from zero through ten. Moving it immediately is simple: call marker.set(7). The setter rejects values outside the range and otherwise stores the new position. That direct call is the right first design when every request happens now and never needs undo. The new requirements are different: collect several moves, perform them later in order, and let the user undo that group in reverse order. The program must also reject a second execution of a move that is already applied.

A vector of destination integers can delay this one operation. However, if the screen later queues a rename or a color change, a vector of integers no longer describes all actions. A growing collection of parallel arrays for action codes and arguments is easy to misalign. The missing idea is to store a request together with the data and behavior needed to carry it out. That stored request is a command. We introduce an interface only because a single queue may need different kinds of requests with the same execute and undo operations.

discussion.question: Why should adding a move to a queue not immediately move the marker?
discussion.answer: The requirement separates scheduling from execution. A queued request records what should happen later; the receiver changes only when the queue executes that request.

before.title: A command has intent before it has a history
paragraphs: Move stores a borrowed Marker reference and a target position. Its constructor records intent but does not move the marker. The reference means there is one actual marker: copying the marker into each command would create private markers and leave the screen unchanged. target_ is stored by value so a later change to a caller variable cannot silently change the queued destination. before_ becomes meaningful only when execute runs. Saving it during construction would record the wrong old position for the second command in a delayed queue.

The interface has virtual execute and undo functions, so callers can use a Command reference without knowing which concrete request it holds. A virtual destructor allows deletion through the base type. Move uses override to ask the compiler to confirm that its functions truly replace those interface functions. std::unique_ptr<Command> owns each queued command. The vector owns its smart pointers, while each command merely borrows the marker. In main the marker is declared before the queue and is destroyed after it, so all borrowed references remain valid.

before.title: Execution has a commit point
paragraphs: Move begins with applied_ false. execute first rejects a repeated call. It then saves the current marker position, asks the marker to accept the target, and only after success sets applied_ true. This last step is a commit point: the flag now says there is a completed change that can be undone. If the setter rejects eleven, the marker remains unchanged and applied_ remains false. before_ may have been refreshed, but it does not authorize undo because the flag is still false.

This order is not cosmetic. Setting applied_ true before the setter succeeds would mark a failed request as part of the undo history. Updating the marker before validating the target would allow an invalid state even if an exception is thrown afterward. Here the setter validates first and then assigns one integer, which cannot throw. The program therefore gives a clear guarantee for a bad target: the visible marker stays as it was. This guarantee depends on the receiver behavior; a command cannot make a partly failing external service atomic merely by adding a bool.

before.title: Undo reverses successful requests in reverse order
paragraphs: The first queued move records zero and sets three. The second records three and sets seven. To reverse the group, undo the second move to restore three, then undo the first to restore zero. The reverse iterators rbegin and rend traverse the vector from its last element toward its first. In (*it)->undo(), *it obtains the unique pointer stored at the iterator position; the arrow accesses the owned command. Iteration changes which command is selected, not who owns it.

An undo operation is permitted only for an applied command. After restoration, applied_ becomes false and another execute is allowed; that is the limited redo behavior of this implementation. Redo reads a new before_ value at execution time. It does not promise to replay the exact historical environment. The design assumes exclusive, ordered changes to this marker while a history is active. If unrelated code changes the marker to nine between execution and undo, blindly restoring before_ can erase that later change. Real editors often route all edits through one history owner or use version checks to detect conflicts.

before.title: Queueing, undo, and transactions are separate promises
paragraphs: The primary queue loop runs commands in order but does not automatically undo earlier commands if a later one fails. A transaction is a group treated as one success or failure under a stated contract. The lab adds a small transaction runner for range failures: it counts successfully applied commands and reverses only that prefix. An empty batch succeeds without changing the marker. A batch containing targets six and eleven returns failure and restores the original zero. This works because the local receiver and undo operations have tightly controlled behavior.

A command can also represent an operation that cannot truly be undone. Sending a message may be followed by a correction, but the recipient may already have read it. A compensation is a new action that tries to offset an earlier effect; it is not time travel. Another option for local state is a snapshot, developed in Chapter 17, which remembers the state instead of how to reverse each action. For this marker, two integers and a flag are cheaper and clearer than a general snapshot system. Choose what must be preserved before promising undo to a user.

before.title: Pattern overview
paragraphs: Let a caller visit a collection through a traversal object instead of reaching into its storage. Each traversal keeps its own position. The EPUB motivates different walks through the same data, including trees and social profiles. The collection produces an iterator suited to its representation. The iterator knows how to test completion, read the current element, and advance. before.title: The problem: callers need readings, not storage details
paragraphs: A measurement log stores a sequence of integer readings. A report must visit the readings in insertion order and compute their total. The simplest loop uses a vector directly, and that is often the best answer when the vector is already part of the public design. The new constraint is that reports should not depend on the storage layout. The log may later use chunks, a file cache, or a filtered view. Reports also need independent positions: one view may be examining the first reading while another has reached the second.

Giving every caller a reference to the internal vector exposes more than traversal. Callers can start depending on contiguous memory, indexing, and mutation details. Copying the entire vector into every report hides storage but can waste memory when readings are numerous. We need a small object that remembers a position and provides the next value without handing over the container. That object is an iterator. The teaching implementation calls it Cursor to emphasize its explicit done, read, and next operations.

discussion.question: Two readers walk the same collection at different speeds. What state must remain separate?
discussion.answer: Each reader needs its own traversal position. They may share the stored readings, but advancing one reader must not advance the other. Changes to the collection need a separate invalidation rule.

before.title: Separate a collection from a position within it
paragraphs: Readings owns its vector and a version number. Cursor borrows the Readings object, stores the version seen at creation, and starts its own index at zero. The collection therefore holds data while each cursor holds traversal state. Copying a cursor copies its position and saved version but still refers to the same owner. Advancing the copy does not advance the original. In the example, one cursor moves to nine while an independent copy still reads four.

The nested class declaration places Cursor inside Readings as part of its interface. A nested class can access the enclosing class private members through an object; it does not carry an implicit enclosing object by magic. owner_ provides that actual object. const Readings& prevents the cursor from modifying the owner through that reference. It does not prevent other code from calling append on the original non-const collection. That distinction is why a read-only reference does not make a changing collection safe by itself.

before.title: An end position exists, but it is not an element
paragraphs: For two readings, legal traversal positions are index zero, index one, and index two as the end marker. done reports true at index two. There is no third reading to return. read calls vector.at, which checks the bound and throws std::out_of_range when asked for the end element. next also rejects an attempt to step beyond end. Empty collections begin at end, so the same loop works without a special branch in the report.

The report loop checks !scan.done before calling read. The exclamation mark means not: it enters the body only while the cursor is not at end. After reading, scan.next advances one position. read returns int by value, so the report receives an independent copy. An element reference could avoid copying a large object, but that reference would introduce its own invalidation and lifetime rules. A copied integer keeps this first traversal interface honest and small. The cursor still borrows the collection and must not outlive it.

paragraphs: For two readings, legal traversal positions are index zero, index one, and index two as the end marker. done reports true at index two. There is no third reading to return. read calls vector.at, which checks the bound and throws std::out_of_range when asked for the end element. next also rejects an attempt to step beyond end. Empty collections begin at end, so the same loop works without a special branch in the report.

The report loop checks !scan.done before calling read. The exclamation mark means not: it enters the body only while the cursor is not at end. After reading, scan.next advances one position. read returns int by value, so the report receives an independent copy. An element reference could avoid copying a large object, but that reference would introduce its own invalidation and lifetime rules. A copied integer keeps this first traversal interface honest and small. The cursor still borrows the collection and must not outlive it.

before.title: A changed collection makes old cursors stale
paragraphs: Invalidation means that an operation has ended a cursor validity under its documented rules. This implementation chooses a strict policy: every successful append invalidates every existing cursor, even if the vector happened to have spare capacity. append first checks that the version counter can be increased without wrapping, then appends the value, then increases the version. If vector growth fails, neither the collection contents nor the version is committed by this append of an integer. A cursor compares its captured version with the current version before done, read, or next proceeds.

A stale cursor is different from a cursor at end. End is a valid position in an unchanged collection. Stale means the view no longer matches the collection generation, even if its numeric index remains within bounds. Merely using at would detect a bad index but would not detect a changed traversal contract. The program checks this difference by creating a cursor, appending twelve, and rejecting use of the old cursor. Version exhaustion is rejected instead of wrapping to an old number that might make a stale cursor look current.

before.title: A safety check cannot bring a dead owner back
paragraphs: The version check reads owner_.stamp_. If the Readings object has already been destroyed, even that first read would use a dangling reference. The check therefore protects against documented mutation while the owner is alive; it is not a general lifetime detector. main declares the collection first and all cursors later, so the collection outlives them. Copy and assignment of Readings are deleted in this example, and it has no implicit move operation. Its identity stays fixed while cursors borrow it.

Alternative designs make different promises. A snapshot cursor could own a copy of the values, remain valid after append, and cost more memory. A cursor holding shared ownership of an immutable collection can extend lifetime without copying its data. Standard-library containers already supply carefully specified iterators; use them when their contracts fit. This Cursor deliberately does not claim to model a standard C++ iterator category: it lacks operator*, operator++, comparison, and the related type information. It teaches the separation of traversal state from storage without pretending to work with every standard algorithm.

before.title: Choose traversal features from the reporting problem
paragraphs: A forward scan is enough for the total. The lab introduces a real new need: show the newest readings first. Its reverse cursor stores the number of elements still available and reads the element at remaining minus one. It checks for zero before subtracting, because size_t is unsigned and zero minus one would wrap to a huge value. Forward and reverse cursors follow the same version policy, so a caller does not need to guess which mutation rules apply.

The primary tests establish behavior for a small deterministic collection, an empty collection, independent positions, end access, end advancement, and stale access. They do not prove thread safety. Concurrent append and read without synchronization can create a data race; a version integer is not a lock. A real reporting subsystem should either prevent concurrent edits during a scan, take a stable snapshot, or define synchronization around both data and cursor checks. The traversal interface makes that choice easier to review, but cannot make it disappear.

discussion.question: Why use remaining minus one for reverse read?
discussion.answer: remaining counts unread elements. For a nonempty view, the next reverse index is one less than that count; checking empty first prevents unsigned underflow.

before.title: Pattern overview
paragraphs: Put the rules for collaboration in one mediator so peer components do not need to know and call each other. The EPUB shows form controls whose mutual dependencies make reuse difficult. Its solution makes a dialog responsible for combined behavior while each control reports its own event through a small interface.

A component completes its local change and notifies a mediator. The mediator interprets the event in the wider context, then calls the components that must react. This central policy replaces peer-to-peer coordination. It does not mean every class belongs in one giant controller; a mediator should cover one coherent collaboration with clear event rules.

before.title: The problem: one form rule spreads across several controls
paragraphs: A save form has a name field, a consent choice, and a save button. The button should be enabled only when the name is nonempty and consent is accepted. An attempted save while disabled must return false and leave the save count unchanged. Start with one function that computes the rule. If the program is just a small procedural form, that single function is enough. The need for a new structure appears when reusable field and button components must participate without learning the private details of one another.

One tempting design gives the name field a button pointer and has it enable the button whenever text appears. Then the consent control also changes the button. The two controls now need to know the same combined rule. If the name field enables the button without checking consent, typing a name bypasses the requirement. If both controls know each other, changes to the form ripple through all of them. We need one owner of the collaboration rule while keeping the controls responsible for their own simple behavior.

before.title: Let components report; let the form decide
paragraphs: A mediator is an object that coordinates the interaction of other objects. Here Form is the mediator. NameField stores text and reports a changed event. SaveButton stores whether it is enabled. Neither component needs to call the other. Form knows the rule that combines a filled name with accepted consent, so its changed function recomputes the button state from current facts.

The small Events interface lets NameField report a change without depending on the concrete Form class. The field receives Events& in its constructor: a required borrowed relationship with no null state. Events has a virtual destructor and a pure virtual changed function. Form implements changed using override, so a misspelled or incompatible replacement is caught during compilation. This interface is justified by reusing the same field with another coordinator. If the form had no reusable components, a direct helper function would be simpler.

before.title: Follow one change from input to visible state
paragraphs: Form::name takes a string by value and moves it into NameField::set. The move permits the string storage to be transferred instead of copied when possible; it does not turn the string into a raw pointer. set compares the new text with the old text. Equal text returns immediately because it creates no new fact for the coordinator. Otherwise the field stores the new value and then calls events_.changed. That order matters: the mediator must observe the updated field, not yesterday’s text.

changed reads name_.filled, combines that result with accepted_ using &&, and calls save_.enable. Logical AND is true only when both conditions are true. The local ready value means the name condition alone; the final expression still checks consent. The button update is silent: enable stores a bool but does not report another event. The event direction therefore ends after one coordination step. A mediator is not a promise that loops cannot occur; these particular method contracts are what prevent a feedback loop.

before.title: Ownership and callbacks must fit together
paragraphs: Form contains NameField and SaveButton by value, so it owns their lifetimes. Its constructor initializes name_ with *this, a reference to the Form being constructed, treated as its Events base. Passing this reference during construction is safe here because the NameField constructor only stores it and does not call changed. Calling back before all Form members had been initialized would make the coordinator read incomplete state. The code deliberately has no such constructor callback.

The field borrows the mediator it lives inside. This creates a relationship cycle in the object graph, but not an ownership cycle: only Form owns the field; the field does not own Form. Copy and assignment are deleted, which also prevents an implicit move constructor in this design. Without that restriction, a default copy of the field reference would still refer to the original Form, and changes in the copied form could update the wrong button. A more flexible movable form would need to rebind every callback relationship during its move operation.

before.title: The coordinator owns policy, not every job
paragraphs: Form::submit checks the current button state and returns false if saving is disabled. The successful path increments saved_, a small local stand-in for completed saves in this demonstration. It does not write a file, send a request, or claim durability. The tests use the count to prove that rejected submissions had no effect. In a real form, the save service belongs behind a separate interface; the mediator can call it, but should not absorb file formats, storage retries, and every other subsystem rule.

Consent changes go through accept, which stores the new bool and calls changed. A repeated accept may recompute the button even if nothing changed; recomputing this pure boolean rule is harmless. The name field avoids equal-text notifications to demonstrate a useful event contract. Neither behavior is inherently more correct. What matters is that listeners know whether setters always notify, notify only on actual change, or never notify. Naming and tests should make the policy visible rather than leave users to infer it from a framework.

before.title: Control the growth of the mediator
paragraphs: When forms gain dozens of unrelated behaviors, the mediator can become one huge object that knows too much. Divide coordination by purpose: a validation controller can decide readiness, a storage service can save, and a page controller can choose which view is shown. The goal is a clear home for a specific collaboration, not one central object for an entire application. Do not make every event a string if a small typed interface can keep mistakes visible to the compiler.

The lab adds a temporary hold flag. A held form must disable save even with valid text and consent; lifting the hold must recompute from the other conditions. This change belongs in the mediator because neither the field nor the button knows what a hold means. The extension tests preserve both old rejection cases and the save count. The same reasoning is useful in an editor, setup wizard, or simulation control panel: components announce local changes, and a coordinator decides what those changes mean together.
