before.title: The problem: remember an interval without breaking its rules
paragraphs: A chart lets a reader select an inclusive interval from zero through one hundred. The low endpoint must never exceed the high endpoint. A change sets both endpoints together, and undo should restore the previous pair. One direct approach keeps two old integer variables beside the user-interface code. That is enough for a single local operation when the state is already public. The problem appears when the selection owns private state and more callers need undo without learning how that state is stored.

Exposing low_ and high_ so a history manager can copy them creates two risks. A caller can change only one endpoint and leave an invalid interval. Also, adding another part of selection state forces every outside snapshot routine to change. The object that understands the rules should produce its own saved record. The history manager should store that record without reading or editing its contents. A saved record with this role is a memento, also called a snapshot.

before.title: Let the state owner define the snapshot boundary
paragraphs: Selection keeps low_ and high_ private. Its set operation accepts both values, validates all conditions, and changes neither member if the pair is invalid. The Snapshot nested class also keeps its two integers private. Its constructor is private, so outside code cannot construct an arbitrary invalid pair disguised as a valid snapshot. friend class Selection grants Selection access to those private members and constructor. Friendship is a specific access permission; it is not inheritance, ownership, or a promise that all surrounding classes can inspect the record.

Snapshot publicly supports copying. This lets a History store snapshots in a vector without seeing their fields. Selection::save builds a snapshot from the current valid pair and returns it by value. Modern C++ can construct that returned value directly in its destination; whether a small copy is removed does not change the ownership contract. The snapshot owns two independent integers, so later edits to Selection cannot change what the snapshot remembers. A snapshot that stored references to live endpoints would fail this basic requirement.

before.title: Restoration should have a clear failure story
paragraphs: restore takes a const Snapshot& and copies both integers back. It borrows the saved record for the duration of the call and leaves that record unchanged. Because these integer assignments cannot allocate or throw, restoration cannot stop between endpoints through a C++ exception in this implementation. This is an exception-safety guarantee for local operations, not a statement that another thread cannot see an intermediate assignment. The program is single-threaded and requires external synchronization if shared.

The snapshot stores the entire selected interval and nothing else. It does not store the chart pixels, a mouse position, a disk file, or the number of saved history entries. Those choices form the snapshot boundary: which state is restored together. Including too little produces inconsistent restoration; including unrelated state makes undo surprisingly broad. Here any Snapshot created by any Selection can be restored into another Selection because every instance uses the same range rules. The test demonstrates that portable value policy. A per-document or per-session policy would need an identity token and an explicit rejection rule.

before.title: The history manager keeps records without opening them
paragraphs: History borrows a Selection and owns a vector of Snapshot values. remember asks the selection for a snapshot and stores it. undo returns false for an empty vector, making the lack of history an ordinary result rather than an exceptional failure. Otherwise it restores the last snapshot and only then removes that snapshot. The order expresses a useful general rule: do not consume the recovery record before the restoration it supports has succeeded.

In this example restoration cannot throw, but retaining the order makes later changes easier to reason about. If snapshots later include a string or collection, restoring field by field could allocate and fail halfway through. A stronger design could build a complete proposed state first and swap it into place with a nonthrowing operation. The caretaker, the common pattern name for a history manager, should not guess how to do that. The object that owns the state must preserve its own invariants during restoration.

before.title: A snapshot is a value, not a rewind button for the world
paragraphs: The sample saves [2,5], changes the selection to [20,40], and restores [2,5]. It also keeps a separate snapshot variable and restores it more than once. This is valid because restore does not consume the snapshot. History choosing to pop its last record is a policy of that history, not a property of all snapshots. A history can instead support named checkpoints, multiple branches, or repeated restore to one baseline. Each needs a clear rule for which records remain available.

Restoring an interval does not undo an exported image that was already sent to another person. A snapshot covers local state inside its declared boundary. It also does not automatically provide persistence across program runs: the program stores C++ values in memory and defines no file format. Persistent snapshots need versioned data, validated loading, and a plan for fields that change between software versions. Calling a memory snapshot a backup would mislead users unless those additional guarantees exist.

before.title: Bound memory growth without weakening the contract
paragraphs: Unlimited history stores more records after every remember call. For two integers this seems cheap, but a rich document may hold large images or trees. A capacity limit is therefore a product choice as well as a memory choice: the user can undo only so far. The lab retains the newest three remembered states. It builds a proposed vector, removes the oldest item if necessary, appends the new snapshot, then swaps the proposed vector into place. If allocation fails before the swap, the original history remains available.

A complete copied snapshot is easiest to reason about but may be costly. An alternative stores only the changed values, called a delta, or uses command-specific undo as in Chapter 14. Another approach shares immutable data between snapshots. These designs can save memory but add dependencies between records or more demanding ownership rules. Measure the actual state size and editing pattern. Do not replace a few cheap copied values with a complicated history graph merely because the latter sounds more advanced.

before.title: Pattern overview
paragraphs: Let interested objects register for events, then notify those objects through one common interface. The teaching problem is a changing audience: the producer should not name every view, logger, or alert class that might need its updates.

The publisher stores registrations. Its event-producing operation walks those registrations and calls the observer interface on each current subscriber. Registration decides who hears an event; virtual dispatch decides how each listener responds. This is the defining Observer connection. A vector, a weak pointer, and a cleanup guard support this implementation but do not define the pattern.

before.question: What problem does Observer address?
before.answer: Let interested objects register for events, then notify those objects through one common interface. The teaching problem is a changing audience: the producer should not name every view, logger, or alert class that might need its updates.

before.question: What is Observer?
before.answer: A listener registered to receive notifications about an event or change.

before.question: What is Weak pointer?
before.answer: A non-owning observer of an object managed by shared ownership.

before.question: What is Reentrancy?
before.answer: Entering an operation again before a previous call to it has finished.

before.question: What is Fail-fast delivery?
before.answer: A policy that stops notifying remaining listeners when a callback fails.

before.question: Does Observer require the publisher to own its subscribers?
before.answer: No. Notification and ownership are separate decisions. The supplied client manages raw-pointer lifetimes; Feed uses weak registrations and temporary ownership during each callback.

before.question: Why can a failed notification leave Total changed?
before.answer: Total adds the reading before its test callback runs. Observer provides delivery structure, not automatic rollback of effects already performed.

Feed keeps weak registrations and locks each one for the duration of its call. A scope guard clears the in-progress flag on all exits. Callback errors stop delivery and propagate without claiming rollback.

after.question: What is Observer?
after.answer: A listener registered to receive notifications about an event or change.

after.question: What is Weak pointer?
after.answer: A non-owning observer of an object managed by shared ownership.

after.question: What is Reentrancy?
after.answer: Entering an operation again before a previous call to it has finished.

after.question: What is Fail-fast delivery?
after.answer: A policy that stops notifying remaining listeners when a callback fails.

after.question: Does Observer require the publisher to own its subscribers?
after.answer: No. Notification and ownership are separate decisions. The supplied client manages raw-pointer lifetimes; Feed uses weak registrations and temporary ownership during each callback.

after.question: Why can a failed notification leave Total changed?
after.answer: Total adds the reading before its test callback runs. Observer provides delivery structure, not automatic rollback of effects already performed.

before.title: The problem: several views need the same new reading
paragraphs: A data feed receives small integer readings between zero and one hundred. A total display needs each new reading; another view may later log values or raise a local alert. The simplest feed directly calls the known views. For a fixed pair that may be enough. The limitation appears when views open and close independently. Adding every view type to the feed couples data delivery to user-interface details, while repeatedly polling the feed can miss changes or waste work.

We need a way for a view to ask for notifications and later disappear without leaving a callable pointer to a destroyed object. A listener is an object that receives an update. A publisher sends updates to registered listeners. The Observer pattern connects these roles through a shared interface so the publisher knows how to notify, but does not need to know each view’s class. Choosing the interface is only the start; the more difficult work is deciding lifetime and behavior during notification.

before.title: Separate registration from ownership
paragraphs: Listener declares virtual update(int), and Total implements it. Feed stores weak_ptr<Listener> values. A weak pointer observes an object managed by shared_ptr without keeping that object alive. main owns the live Total through shared_ptr; Feed owns only registration entries. Before calling a listener, publish uses weak.lock to obtain a temporary shared_ptr. A successful lock keeps that particular listener alive until the local live pointer is released. A failed lock means the listener has expired, so the feed skips it.

The statement if (auto live = weak.lock()) both creates the temporary pointer and tests whether it is nonempty. That C++ condition keeps the temporary in scope for the controlled statement. The arrow calls update through the live base-class pointer, choosing the concrete listener function during execution. The compiler checks the shared interface and override signature earlier. Expiration is a normal condition, not an exception. The primary example deliberately destroys one subscriber before publication to show that a registration need not become a dangling raw pointer.

before.title: Registration rules prevent surprises
paragraphs: subscribe rejects an empty shared pointer, because a null registration has no useful meaning. It scans existing entries and returns if the same live object is already registered. Subscribing twice therefore produces one update, not two. Expired entries remain in the primary vector but are skipped during publication. This makes the small example simple; a long-lived feed with many short-lived views should periodically remove expired entries so its registration list does not grow forever.

The implementation forbids changing the registration list while it is publishing. subscribe checks notifying_ before doing anything else, even before duplicate detection. This policy protects iteration from vector changes and makes callback behavior predictable. The lab adds unsubscribe with the same rule. A different design could queue registration changes or publish through a stable snapshot of registrations, but then it must state whether a removed listener receives the current event. There is no universal answer that all observers share.

before.title: Reentrancy is a second call before the first has finished
paragraphs: A callback can call back into its publisher. If a listener tries feed.publish(1) while handling an earlier publication, the second call is reentrant: the first publish has not returned. Unrestricted recursion can create surprising order, repeated updates, or unbounded calls. This feed rejects nested publish with logic_error. A listener may catch that error and continue, as the primary test does, or allow it to propagate. The behavior is chosen deliberately instead of being an accidental consequence of recursive calls.

The notifying_ flag is set only after input validation and the reentrancy guard. A local Reset object borrows that flag and clears it in its destructor. Its destructor runs on normal return and while an exception unwinds the stack. This is resource acquisition is initialization applied to temporary state, not only memory: the local object owns the duty to reset the flag. Without it, a throwing listener could leave notifying_ true and make every later publication look nested even though the old call had already ended.

before.title: Failure during delivery is not an all-or-nothing update
paragraphs: Total first adds the reading to sum and then invokes an optional after callback. In the failure test, adding two changes the total from seven to nine, then after throws. Feed does not catch and continue to later listeners; it propagates the exception and stops the current delivery. Earlier listeners and the throwing listener may already have changed their own state. The Reset destructor clears the flag, so a later publication can run. The next reading of one makes the tested total ten.

This policy is called fail-fast delivery: stop when a callback fails. It is not atomic delivery, in which every listener either receives the change or no listener does. The latter would need much stronger coordination and often cannot be promised for arbitrary outside code. An alternative feed might collect callback errors and continue notifying other listeners. That favors availability but changes error reporting and ordering. In either case, identify whether the feed stores a new reading before publishing and how subscribers recover missed updates. The sample passes event values and keeps no authoritative reading history.

before.title: Keep callback captures inside a known lifetime
paragraphs: Total exposes a std::function<void()> named after solely as a test hook. The empty wrapper means no extra action. The lambda written [&] borrows local objects, including the feed, from main. Those locals remain alive whenever the callback is invoked in this program. Feed itself must stay alive through every active publish call; locking a listener does not keep the publisher alive. Feed deletes copying and assignment and has no implicit move operation, so a callback cannot replace its registration storage by assigning another Feed. Capturing a shared pointer by value inside an object it owns could instead create an ownership cycle. Capturing a short-lived local by reference and invoking it later would leave a dangling reference. A callback is executable state, so its captures deserve the same ownership review as normal members.

The example is single-threaded. weak_ptr provides lifetime coordination for managed objects, but the listener vector, notifying_ flag, and Total::sum are not protected for concurrent access. The total uses int for a small bounded demonstration sequence; an unbounded real stream would require an overflow policy or a wider checked total. Use the pattern to separate interest from production, then write precise rules for delivery, registration, expiration, failure, and concurrency. A diagram with one arrow to each listener is not a substitute for those contracts.

paragraphs: Make the same public object respond differently as its current mode changes. The problem is not merely storing a mode name. It is keeping each mode’s behavior and transition rules together as state-dependent decisions spread across a growing program.

A context holds one current state object and delegates state-dependent work through a shared State interface. before.title: The problem: one session, different rules at different times
paragraphs: A local data-import session begins idle. A begin event makes it active. A finish event is accepted only while active and moves it to done. A reset event is accepted only while done and returns it to idle. Every other event is rejected without changing the session. These rules form a finite-state machine: a system with a limited set of named states and permitted changes between them. A state is the current mode; a transition is an allowed change of mode in response to an event.

The simplest implementation uses an enum for the current mode and a switch for each event. That is a good choice for this three-state machine if behavior stays small. The difficulty appears when each state gains different begin, finish, status, timeout, and cleanup behavior, and those decisions spread across many switches. A maintainer can update one switch but forget another. Grouping behavior by state becomes useful when the behavior that belongs together is easier to review in one place. The object-based solution here shows that growth path without claiming it is the shortest solution to three transitions.

before.title: A state object supplies behavior for the current mode
paragraphs: State declares two operations: name and next. name describes the current mode. next receives an Event and returns either an owned proposed next state or no state for rejection. Idle, Active, and Done each implement this interface. Each class therefore gathers the rules for events received while that state is current. before.title: Do not destroy the state while its method is still running
paragraphs: A dangerous implementation lets a state call a context setter that immediately deletes the current state. That setter may delete the very object whose member function is still executing. Some carefully restricted cases can avoid further access, but it is a fragile rule to maintain: adding a log that reads a member afterward can use a dead object. This design avoids the entire hazard. next only returns a proposal. Session waits for the virtual call to finish and then replaces state_.

The assignment state_ = std::move(proposed) transfers ownership of the new state into Session and destroys the previously owned state. std::move does not itself move bytes or call a transition; it enables the unique pointer’s move assignment. The old handler has already returned at this point. If there is no proposal, send returns false without changing state_. Session deletes copying and assignment and provides no move operation, keeping the non-null state invariant straightforward. A movable Session would need a documented rule for its moved-from state or a safe reinitialization strategy.

before.title: Rejected events are part of the model
paragraphs: There are three states and three event values, so the primary behavior table has nine state-event combinations. Only three are accepted. The other six are not omissions; they are defined rejections. main checks all nine combinations while moving through the normal cycle. In idle, finish and reset are false. In active, begin and reset are false. In done, begin and finish are false. Each accepted event is followed by a state-name check, so a return value alone cannot hide a wrong destination.

This model does not perform a real import, start a thread, or wait for a file. It isolates transition logic for study. A real asynchronous import needs a rule for who sends finish and how a late completion is handled after cancellation. A generation identifier can distinguish a completion from the current run and one from an old run. Adding that protection requires a concrete asynchronous requirement; it should not be implied by a state diagram that only contains begin and finish arrows.

before.title: State and Strategy solve different change problems
paragraphs: A strategy is a selected way to perform a task, such as choosing a sorting or compression rule. It is normally selected because a caller wants a different algorithm. State represents a mode governed by the object’s history and permitted events. Their class shapes can look alike because both delegate through an interface. Their contracts differ: selecting any next strategy may be acceptable, while jumping from idle to done without begin and finish would violate this session’s protocol.

For a tiny stable machine, a transition table or switch remains easier to scan than several classes and heap allocations. Choose State when state-specific behavior grows enough to justify grouping it, or when ownership of mode-specific data becomes important. The lab adds cancel only from active to idle. The key work is not adding one enum word; it is preserving the existing transitions, rejecting cancel from idle and done, and documenting what cancellation means. Testing the full expanded table reveals accidental new transitions that a single happy-path test would miss.

before.title: Pattern overview
paragraphs: Let one object use different ways of doing the same task without embedding every algorithm in that object. The changing part is the calculation or policy; the surrounding workflow should remain stable when another supported method is added.

The context holds an object through a shared strategy interface. The client chooses a concrete strategy and supplies it to the context. When work arrives, the context calls that interface rather than testing every algorithm name. Replacing the installed object changes the chosen algorithm without replacing the context. This is composition: one object performs part of its job by using another object.

paragraphs: A room monitor receives a small batch of whole-number readings. Each reading is from 0 through 1000. A batch contains 1 through 1000 readings. The ordinary screen shows the average, rounded down. During a review, an operator wants the highest reading instead. Both views use the same batch. Neither view may edit the stored readings. The input limits keep arithmetic predictable and make a missing batch an error rather than a made-up zero.

before.title: The specific limit: unrelated changes share one function
paragraphs: Now a third team wants the middle reading after sorting. A fourth wants a calibrated result with stored settings. Each addition changes the same selection function. A new branch can accidentally skip shared validation. Sorting the original batch to find the middle also changes data that another screen expected to keep in arrival order. These are concrete costs, not proof that every if statement is bad.

We need a small interchangeable rule, called a strategy. The monitor keeps the stable work: check inputs, then ask its current rule for one answer. Each rule owns its calculation. The caller chooses the rule because the caller knows what the operator requested. This arrangement is the Strategy pattern. Its purpose is replaceable behavior. The number of classes is a consequence of that need, not the goal.

before.title: A contract larger than a function signature
paragraphs: Estimate declares value. The const reference borrows a vector and forbids changing its elements through that reference. The final const describes the Estimate object used for the call: value promises not to change its ordinary members. These are two separate const promises. The function returns a new integer value, so its result does not borrow storage from the vector.

The interface also has a written contract. Its caller supplies a nonempty validated batch, and the rule returns a whole-number estimate without changing that batch. Average and Highest rely on that precondition. Calling either concrete rule directly with an empty vector violates the contract: Average divides by zero; Highest would dereference an end iterator. The monitor is the intended public entry point for untrusted data. An interface does not cause the compiler to check these meaning-level rules.

Average uses integer division. With 1, 2, and 9, the sum is 12 and the answer is 4. With 1 and 2, the answer is 1. This is deliberate downward rounding for nonnegative values. At the largest accepted batch, the sum is at most 1,000,000, which fits the required ordinary int implementations with at least 32 bits. If the environment had only a 16-bit int, this chapter's arithmetic requirements would need a wider type. Highest uses max_element, which returns an iterator pointing at the largest element; the leading star reads the pointed-to integer.

before.title: What the compiler fixes and execution selects
paragraphs: During compilation, the compiler checks the override signatures and that Estimate has the requested operation. A virtual call through rule_ selects the implementation belonging to the actual object during execution. Replacing Average with Highest changes the selected object, not the code of Monitor::read. A compiler may optimize a call whose target it can prove, but the program must keep the same observable behavior.

A unique_ptr is the sole owning handle. Monitor receives that handle by value and moves it into rule_. std::move permits ownership transfer; it does not call the estimate or copy its readings. The arrow in rule_->value reaches the object owned by the handle and calls its method. On replacement, the previous strategy is destroyed. Monitor explicitly deletes copying; those user-declared copy operations also suppress its implicit move operations. The monitor itself therefore keeps a stable identity, while its strategy can be replaced. This avoids leaving a moved-from monitor with an empty rule. The virtual destructor makes destruction through the base type reach the complete derived object. Data is borrowed only for the duration of read; ownership of the strategy lasts until replacement or monitor destruction.

before.title: Failure boundaries and a smaller alternative
paragraphs: select checks the proposed handle before assigning it. A null request throws, while the old strategy remains usable. read validates every reading before calling the strategy. These boundaries make failure local: a bad sample cannot partly sort or partly accumulate shared state inside the strategy. The current calculations themselves have no external effects. A future rule that writes a file would need a stronger contract about partial failure.

For a single stateless operation, a function pointer, a lambda, or std::function can express Strategy with less class code. A template parameter is attractive when the rule is fixed at compilation and speed or inlining matters. The virtual interface earns its place when selection occurs during execution, rule objects hold settings, or several operations belong to one rule. Do not add a strategy for each constant. A named parameter can represent a threshold without creating a new type.

In a long-lived monitor, replacement also raises a timing question: can one thread replace a rule while another calls read? This example is single-threaded and makes no such guarantee. A mutex, immutable shared snapshot, or an event-loop rule could define a safe policy. Merely using a smart pointer does not synchronize access to the member that holds it.

before.title: Pattern overview
paragraphs: Keep the required order of a process in one place while letting related implementations supply selected steps. The motivating failure is duplicated workflows: one copy receives a validation or ordering repair while another quietly keeps the old behavior.

An abstract base class defines the complete algorithm as a template method. That method calls ordinary shared operations, required virtual steps, and optional virtual hooks in a fixed order. A concrete subclass supplies the varying steps. The base algorithm calls into the subclass at those designated points. before.question: What is Template Method?
before.answer: A base-class operation that fixes a sequence while letting derived classes replace selected steps.

before.question: What is Hook?
before.answer: An optional extension point with a useful default or an empty default action.

before.question: What is Postcondition?
before.answer: A rule that must be true when an operation successfully returns.

before.question: What is Name hiding?
before.answer: A derived declaration prevents ordinary lookup from finding a same-named base declaration; it is not necessarily an override.

before.question: Why does run validate all raw input before calling convert once?
before.answer: That is the workflow contract. With {3,-1}, no conversion may run before rejection. Combining the loops would change observable behavior for a step with side effects.

before.question: Does an optional hook mean subclasses may reorder the process?
before.answer: No. A hook changes behavior at its designated point. The template method retains the call order; suffix runs only after all conversions succeed.

before.title: Two imports must follow the same rules
paragraphs: An import tool receives whole-number readings from 0 through 100. One input source already uses the desired units. Another source needs every value doubled. Each result is a space-separated string; the doubled form ends with scaled. Reject an empty input and reject any out-of-range reading. A bad reading late in the batch must be found before any conversion begins. The caller must receive a complete string or an exception, never a partly formatted result.

A simple implementation writes one loop for the ordinary input and copies it for the doubled input. The excerpt shows the ordinary conversion after validation. This is easy to understand at first. But when the team adds a full-batch validation rule, both import functions need the same repair. If only one is repaired, the sources obey different rules even though their only intended difference is a unit conversion.

before.title: The limitation calls for one fixed sequence
paragraphs: The repeated sequence is validate all inputs, convert each value, check each converted value, and finish the string. The differing step is how one valid integer becomes another. The Template Method pattern places the sequence in a base class and lets derived classes supply selected steps. Here Import::run is the template method. The word template means a shared plan of steps; it does not refer to C++ template parameters.

convert is a required step: every concrete import must supply it. suffix is an optional hook: the base implementation returns an empty string, so an ordinary import need not override it. DoubleImport changes both conversion and suffix. Optional does not mean uncontrolled. A hook must still obey the documented contract and must not quietly perform a second import or change shared input.

before.title: Where control moves and where it does not
paragraphs: The caller invokes run. run first walks the full input to check every raw value. Only after that pass succeeds does it create the local stream and call convert for each input. The virtual call selects the actual derived implementation. Control returns to run, which checks that the result lies from 0 through 200 and appends it. The final suffix call happens once after the loop. The base therefore owns the order while the derived class owns a small part of the meaning.

The two passes are deliberate. In a one-pass implementation, convert(3) could run before discovering -1 in the next position. For our pure conversion methods that would not change external state, but the order would violate the stated guarantee. A future conversion with an audit counter would expose that difference. Define order before optimizing away a pass. The cost is one extra linear walk; it does not copy the vector.

input is a const reference, so run borrows existing readings. Each raw loop variable is an integer copy. value is another local integer, held const because the result should not change after the conversion call. The stream owns the characters accumulated so far. Its exception mask enables badbit and failbit exceptions: an output failure must throw rather than silently leave a partial stream result. result.str() returns a string value. If conversion throws or violates the result range, stack cleanup destroys the local stream, and no partial string is returned. This does not undo outside effects a derived step might already have made.

before.title: A skeleton is a contract, not a security barrier
paragraphs: run is nonvirtual, so calls through Import use this exact sequence. A derived class can declare a same-named nonvirtual member and hide it for calls made through that derived type. That is name hiding, not overriding. Our final concrete classes do not do so, and normal clients use the inherited run. If a framework needs the compiler to forbid overriding an already virtual public entry point, virtual plus final is an available design. It still does not prevent unrelated methods from doing other work.

Protected access lets derived classes implement and use steps without advertising them as normal public operations. A derived override may be private, as it is here: access checking uses the base declaration at the call inside Import, and virtual dispatch can reach the private override. override asks the compiler to verify that the method truly matches a virtual base declaration. It prevents mistakes such as accidentally omitting a trailing const and introducing a different function.

At compilation, types and signatures are checked. During execution, run chooses step implementations from the actual import object. The object must already be fully constructed. Do not call a pure virtual conversion from the base constructor to “test” it: construction-time virtual behavior does not act like a call on a completed derived object. Validate construction data without relying on not-yet-constructed derived behavior.

before.title: When composition gives a better boundary
paragraphs: Template Method fits a family of closely related processes whose ordering is stable and whose variation belongs in a few well-defined steps. Its cost is inheritance coupling: changing the base sequence changes every derived import. Adding many hooks can make the sequence hard to reason about because every empty-looking call may run unknown derived work.

If callers need to exchange the conversion while keeping the same importer object, inject a Strategy instead. If there are just two lines of differing math, pass a callable to one ordinary function. If whole workflows differ in ordering, forcing them into one inherited skeleton may hide the true differences. Choose a stable sequence first, then decide how much extension it needs.

This example checks both sides of the extension point: raw values are preconditions, converted values are postconditions, which are rules that must hold when a step returns. Runtime range checks catch some bad implementations, such as BrokenImport returning 201. They cannot prove that doubled units have the right business meaning. Keep value-based tests alongside these general contract checks.

before.title: Pattern overview
paragraphs: Add operations across stable element types without putting every report inside those classes. The design makes new operations easier, but each new element type requires every visitor to account for it.

Each element accepts a visitor through a shared interface. Its concrete accept implementation passes itself to the visitor entry point for that precise element type. The visitor supplies the operation for every supported type. Selection depends on both the actual element and actual visitor, a mechanism called double dispatch. Traversal decides which element comes next; acceptance decides which type-specific operation runs.

before.title: The problem: the parts stay familiar while reports multiply
paragraphs: A workshop order contains two kinds of item: a group of bolts counted by pieces, and a cable measured in whole metres. Each quantity must be between zero and one hundred. A price report charges five cents per bolt and forty cents per metre. The total cannot exceed one million cents. Direct price methods on Bolts and Cable are a reasonable first design when price is the one operation every item must offer. The next requests are labels, packing summaries, and audit reports, each with different output needs.

Adding every report as another virtual member makes stable data types change whenever a reporting team needs a new operation. A large switch on a type code moves the work outside the classes but loses compiler-checked access to the distinct data of each kind. We need to let an outside operation receive the exact kind of part while callers still traverse a mixed list through the common Part interface. The Visitor pattern provides this connection, at a cost: the set of element types becomes explicit in the visitor interface.

paragraphs: Visitor declares two overloaded visit functions: one taking const Bolts& and one taking const Cable&. Overloading means several functions share a name but have different parameter lists. Part declares accept(Visitor&) const. Each concrete element implements accept and calls visitor.visit with a reference to itself. The const qualifier at the end means this accepting operation cannot change the element through its ordinary members. The visitor reference is not const, because a report visitor may update its own running result. before.title: Why a single overloaded call is not enough
paragraphs: Imagine a Part& variable that actually refers to a Bolts object. Calling visitor.visit(part) cannot select visit(const Bolts&) merely because the runtime object happens to be bolts. Overload resolution, the choice among same-name functions, uses the expression’s static type during compilation. Here the static type is Part&, and Visitor does not offer a Part overload. A downcast at every caller would move type-checking knowledge into all loops, defeating the goal of a common traversal.

Instead the loop calls part->accept(price). Virtual dispatch chooses Bolts::accept during execution because the actual element is Bolts. Inside that member, *this has the type const Bolts, so the compiler selects visit(const Bolts&) when compiling that function. Calling the selected virtual visit then dispatches to the implementation belonging to the actual visitor object, Price. The behavior depends on both the element kind and visitor kind. This two-stage selection is called double dispatch. It combines static overload choice with virtual calls; it does not make ordinary C++ overload resolution dynamic.

before.title: Follow ownership without giving it to the visitor
paragraphs: The parts vector owns unique_ptr<Part> values whose actual objects are Bolts and Cable. Part has a virtual destructor so destroying an owning base pointer properly destroys the complete concrete object. Price is a separate local object in main. During accept it borrows each part through a const reference. It does not retain those references, own the parts, or change their quantities. After traversal, the visitor owns only its numeric result.

The forward declarations class Bolts and class Cable tell the compiler that those type names exist before Visitor uses references to them. A reference declaration does not need the complete class layout. The later class definitions provide constructors, getters, and accept bodies. This arrangement resolves the header dependency between the visitor interface and its element types. In a multi-file program, separate headers and forward declarations keep that dependency controlled; putting every implementation in one header can make every report change trigger broad recompilation.

before.title: The price calculation also needs ordinary correctness
paragraphs: Design structure does not make arithmetic automatically safe. Constructors reject negative quantities and quantities above one hundred. Each price term is therefore bounded before multiplication: at most five hundred cents for bolts or four thousand cents for cable. Price::add checks whether the accumulated total exceeds one million minus the next nonnegative term. Only then does it add. Checking before addition avoids computing an overflowed result and trying to diagnose it afterward. The chosen limits fit the required int range on the documented compiler platform.

The sample order contains three bolts and two metres of cable. The terms are fifteen and eighty, so the result is ninety-five cents. A fresh visitor starts at zero; a zero-quantity element changes nothing. For the limit test, two hundred fifty visits to a one-hundred-metre cable reach exactly one million. The next visit throws and leaves the old total intact. The visitor therefore has its own invariant and failure policy, separate from those of the elements. Reusing the same Price visitor for another order would accumulate into the previous result unless the caller deliberately creates a new visitor.

before.title: Choose which direction of change should be easy
paragraphs: Adding Labels in the lab changes no Bolts, Cable, or Part class. Labels implements both visits and appends strings with quantities and unit names. The same traversal works. However, adding a new element kind such as Paint requires a new visit overload in the Visitor interface and an implementation in every concrete visitor. This can be useful: the compiler forces every operation to decide how to handle Paint. It can also be costly when new element kinds arrive frequently and the operation set barely changes.

C++17 offers another option for a closed set of types: std::variant<BoltsData, CableData> can store exactly one alternative, and std::visit selects a callable for the active alternative. This can avoid a heap allocation and a virtual base hierarchy for simple value data. It still makes the type set explicit, and visitors must handle its alternatives. Ordinary virtual members remain simpler when new types are common and the operation set is stable. Visitor is a tradeoff between these directions of change, not a general rule to move every method out of its class.

before.title: Use the taught patterns to make specific decisions
paragraphs: This capstone is an original integration of earlier lessons, not another program from the attachments. Return to Chapter 6 for Adapter, Chapter 20 for Strategy, Chapter 10 for Facade, and Chapter 19 for the distinction between a state machine and the State pattern. The workshop scenario gives those ideas one shared call path: normalize a reading, apply the selected alert rule, commit accepted records, and produce a report.

The strongest direct pattern match is Strategy: Monitor owns an AlertRule, delegates classification to alert, and replaces that object without changing ingestion. AtLeast is the first concrete strategy; the lab adds OutsideBand. SampleAdapter preserves Adapter's translation responsibility as a value-conversion helper, without the attachment's Target inheritance or wrapped Adaptee object. ReportFacade preserves a simple reporting entry point, while its small subsystem consists of history access, counting, and formatting. These are deliberate reductions in structure, not evidence that a suggestive class name alone establishes a pattern.

Choose each boundary from the requirement that motivates it. Mixed units require translation; replaceable alert policies require an interchangeable operation; repeated reporting needs one formatting contract. The four lifecycle states need checked transitions, but their small behavior does not justify polymorphic state objects. Staging a vector before a swap supplies exception safety; it does not automatically introduce Command or Memento. The pattern-choice matrix makes both the selections and the omissions explicit.

before.title: The job: trust the whole path, not just the temperature formula
paragraphs: A small teaching workshop records temperatures from benches that use two sensor formats. Some readings arrive in degrees Celsius, marked C. Others arrive in degrees Fahrenheit, marked F. The operator starts a session, admits batches of readings, pauses to change the alert rule, resumes work, and stops the session. A report must show what the program accepted and what decision it made at that time. This is a teaching monitor, not equipment that protects people or controls a heater.

The hard part is not one calculation. It is keeping several promises together. A unit conversion must happen before a rule judges the temperature. An invalid batch must add nothing. A rule change must affect future readings without rewriting history. A stopped session must remain stopped. An object must not use a rule that has already been destroyed. The capstone joins these concerns in one complete program whose printed report is checked against an exact string.

The input is a vector of RawSample values supplied by the program. Each value contains an integer sequence identifier, a number, and a unit character. Identifiers must be positive and increase across the entire session, including within one batch. Accepted temperatures must lie from -40 through 125 Celsius, including both endpoints. The monitor stores at most eight readings so every full history is small enough to inspect. Empty batches are allowed only while running and change nothing.

We deliberately keep file reading, clocks, sensor drivers, threads, and network calls outside this program. They would add failure modes that hide the design lesson. A real integration can place those concerns before the adapter. It must define its own packet, timing, and recovery contracts. The complete C++ program here already has a useful boundary: either a supplied batch becomes accepted history in full, or the monitor keeps its old history.

after.title: The job: trust the whole path, not just the temperature formula
paragraphs: A small teaching workshop records temperatures from benches that use two sensor formats. Some readings arrive in degrees Celsius, marked C. Others arrive in degrees Fahrenheit, marked F. The operator starts a session, admits batches of readings, pauses to change the alert rule, resumes work, and stops the session. A report must show what the program accepted and what decision it made at that time. This is a teaching monitor, not equipment that protects people or controls a heater.

The hard part is not one calculation. It is keeping several promises together. A unit conversion must happen before a rule judges the temperature. An invalid batch must add nothing. A rule change must affect future readings without rewriting history. A stopped session must remain stopped. An object must not use a rule that has already been destroyed. The capstone joins these concerns in one complete program whose printed report is checked against an exact string.

The input is a vector of RawSample values supplied by the program. Each value contains an integer sequence identifier, a number, and a unit character. Identifiers must be positive and increase across the entire session, including within one batch. Accepted temperatures must lie from -40 through 125 Celsius, including both endpoints. The monitor stores at most eight readings so every full history is small enough to inspect. Empty batches are allowed only while running and change nothing.

We deliberately keep file reading, clocks, sensor drivers, threads, and network calls outside this program. They would add failure modes that hide the design lesson. A real integration can place those concerns before the adapter. It must define its own packet, timing, and recovery contracts. The complete C++ program here already has a useful boundary: either a supplied batch becomes accepted history in full, or the monitor keeps its old history.

before.title: Stage one: the useful ten-line idea and its first failures
paragraphs: The first reasonable design is a loop that compares each number with a limit and prints a label. If every input is valid Celsius and nothing must be remembered, that loop is enough. Do not start with an inheritance tree. Begin by stating the assumptions that make this small design correct: one known unit, one rule, no paused state, and no requirement to reject a whole batch together.

The excerpt below shows the first design. It is intentionally an incomplete illustration, not the delivered executable. With the Fahrenheit reading 100 F, it prints ALERT because 100 is greater than or equal to 80. But 100 F is about 37.8 C, which is below the intended 80 C limit. The comparison is mathematically valid and still answers the wrong question. The missing assumption is the unit of the value.

Adding a unit conversion inside the loop fixes this one error. Later a report and a replay tool also need the same conversion. Copying the formula into all three callers creates three places to disagree about unknown units and valid ranges. A named adapter now earns its place: it turns the outside representation into one internal Sample representation and checks the boundary once. Its purpose is agreement, not the extra class syntax.

The next failure appears when a batch contains a valid first item and a bad second item. Appending directly to live history leaves the first item stored even though the whole request is rejected. That result violates the batch contract. A temporary proposed history, followed by one commit step, fixes the actual problem. Only after these concrete failures do we introduce the larger structure in the finished program.

before.title: Stage two: name the data before spreading behavior
paragraphs: RawSample and Sample are small data types with public fields. A raw sample still carries its unit. A normalized sample has a field named celsius, so later code does not need to guess. Record adds the decision made when that sample entered the monitor. Storing this decision matters: a later rule may classify the same number differently, but the old record is an account of what happened earlier.

The adapter first rejects nonpositive identifiers and nonfinite input values. A finite value is an ordinary bounded number rather than infinity or NaN. NaN means not a number. Ordinary comparisons with NaN do not behave like a simple out-of-range test: both NaN < -40 and NaN > 125 are false. That is why the program uses std::isfinite as well as comparisons. It checks the converted value too, because arithmetic on an extreme finite input can produce infinity.

For Fahrenheit, subtract 32, multiply by 5, then divide by 9. The constants have decimal points so the operations use floating-point arithmetic. Writing 5 / 9 first with two integer operands produces zero. Therefore (value - 32) * (5 / 9) produces zero for every ordinary finite value. The correct source keeps the intended order and floating-point operands visible. The uppercase letters C and F are the only supported tags; guessing a unit after receiving K would conceal a data error.

The allowed range is a program contract, not a claim about every real sensor. The boundary checks apply to the represented floating-point result. An outside device that needs tolerance near a physical limit requires a written tolerance policy and tests; silently adding a small epsilon can admit forbidden values. This example uses exact easy-to-check Fahrenheit cases, 176 F and 212 F, to test normalization to 80 C and 100 C.

before.title: Stage three: two real changes justify one replaceable rule
paragraphs: A fixed threshold is still a good implementation for a workshop with one permanent policy. Here the operator must change the policy between batches, and the lab adds a different kind of rule. If that change requires editing conversion, history, and reporting, the boundaries are wrong. We isolate the question that varies: given one normalized sample, should this reading be marked as an alert?

AlertRule describes that question through a virtual function. Virtual means the call chooses the implementation associated with the actual object at execution time. The compiler checks that AtLeast supplies a function with the declared shape; override asks it to catch a mismatch. The = 0 makes the base operation abstract: an AlertRule by itself has no answer. The monitor calls through the shared interface and does not inspect which concrete rule it owns.

The parameter const Sample& is a borrowed view of the existing sample, not a copied sample and not ownership of it. Const prevents changes to that sample through the parameter. The second const, after the parameter list, promises not to change ordinary fields of the rule through this call. Noexcept promises that this operation will not let an exception escape. It does not prove that a rule is correct or free from side effects. A rule that violates noexcept by throwing terminates the program; it does not produce an ordinary rejected batch.

The design contract therefore adds a behavioral rule: judging a sample must have no outside side effects. AtLeast merely compares two numbers and meets that promise. Logging from inside alert, incrementing an external counter, or sending a message would weaken the all-or-nothing story even if records rolled back. If rules later need historical context, change the interface deliberately and review how that context participates in a transaction. Do not hide new state behind mutable fields.

AtLeast stores an inclusive Celsius limit. A reading equal to the limit is an alert. Its constructor rejects a nonfinite or out-of-range limit before the rule can enter service. An alternative is a function object or std::function with a documented signature. That can be simpler for a few stateless policies. The explicit interface here makes ownership, replacement, and a separately named lab extension easy to inspect; it is not a demand that every comparison become polymorphic.

before.title: Stage four: permitted actions belong to an explicit state
paragraphs: Two booleans such as started and paused allow confusing combinations unless every caller is careful. A stopped flag adds still more combinations. A finite-state machine replaces that loose collection with one named state and a defined set of transitions. Finite means there are only a fixed number of possible states. Transition means a permitted change from one state to another after an action.

The monitor begins idle. Start moves idle to running. Pause moves running to paused. Resume moves paused to running. Stop moves either running or paused to stopped. Stopped is final for that object: create a new Monitor to begin another session. Ingest is legal only in running. Replacing the rule is legal in idle or paused. Reporting is a read operation and is permitted in any state.

Every transition checks its precondition before assigning state_. A precondition is something the caller must make true before the operation. Calling resume while idle throws a logic_error and leaves the state idle. A caller should not repair this by forcing the state field. The field is private precisely so a public operation remains the single place that enforces the rule.

An enum class and short member functions are sufficient here. The identifier State names an enum; this is not the polymorphic State pattern from Chapter 19 or the attachment's State, ConcreteStateA, and ConcreteStateB class family. Monitor checks state_ directly instead of delegating requests to a current state object. The State pattern becomes useful when each state has substantial independent behavior, many operations, or state-specific data. Our four states control only a few gates, and a class tree would make the program harder to follow. The state diagram describes behavior without dictating a particular implementation technique.

before.title: Stage five: validation, a proposed history, and a commit point
paragraphs: Monitor::ingest first checks running state and spare capacity. The capacity test subtracts the current record count from eight before comparing the incoming batch size. This is safe because every accepted history already has at most eight records. The operation then copies records_ into a local vector named staged. All further changes go to this proposed history while the real history remains available unchanged.

The range-based for loop reads one raw item at a time. In for (const auto& raw : batch), the colon means take each element from batch. Auto asks the compiler to infer the element type. The ampersand makes raw a reference to that element; const prevents this loop from changing it. Conversion returns a new Sample value called s. Each accepted identifier must exceed the last staged identifier, so the check catches both old duplicates and duplicates introduced earlier in this same batch.

After conversion and order checks, the monitor calls the rule and appends a Record to staged. Only when the loop finishes does records_.swap(staged) exchange the two vector contents. With the standard allocator used here, vector swap is nonthrowing. This is the commit point: before it, records_ is the old history; after it, records_ is the complete new history. The local staged vector then owns the old storage and destroys it when the function returns.

If copying, conversion, order validation, or appending throws before the swap, local cleanup destroys staged and records_ keeps its old contents. This is the strong exception guarantee for the monitor history: failure leaves the observable stored history unchanged. It is a form of rollback achieved by delaying changes, not by trying to undo half a loop. The supplied rules have no outside effects, so there is no external work to reverse.

The guarantee has limits. It does not make the program recover from termination, a process crash, or a defective rule that breaks its contract. It does not write durable records to disk. It does not undo a message sent by a future callback. Strong exception safety concerns ordinary C++ exception flow for the objects covered by the contract. Naming the scope of the promise prevents a useful local technique from being mistaken for a complete database transaction.

before.title: Stage six: ownership and reports without hidden lifetime traps
paragraphs: A Monitor owns exactly one rule through std::unique_ptr<AlertRule>. Ownership means responsibility for ending the resource lifetime. Unique means this pointer cannot be copied to create another owner. The constructor receives an owning pointer by value and moves it into rule_. std::move allows ownership transfer; it does not create a second rule. The monitor rejects a missing pointer so later calls need not repeatedly test for null.

The virtual destructor on AlertRule makes deletion through the base pointer reach the derived destructor. Replacing the owning pointer destroys the old rule after the replacement has passed the state and null checks. Destroying the Monitor destroys its remaining rule and its vector. The LifetimeRule used in checks borrows a flag that remains alive outside the monitor scope. Its destructor changes that flag, letting a test observe real cleanup without assuming that absence of a crash proves correctness.

A Monitor itself cannot be copied or moved. The four declarations ending in = delete make those operations compile-time errors. An automatic move would empty the old rule pointer while leaving the old state possibly running; calling ingest on that moved-from object could then follow a null pointer. For this session object, a fixed identity is the simpler contract. Moving a unique_ptr that owns a Monitor would still transfer its handle without moving the Monitor object. The type-trait static_assert checks verify these restrictions during compilation; they remain active regardless of NDEBUG. The small Sample and Record value types can still move safely because their fields preserve valid values.

ReportFacade supplies one simple request, summary, over history access, row formatting, and alert counting. It borrows a const Monitor for the duration of the call and returns an independent string. The caller need not know how rows are traversed or how counts are formed. A free function would be a reasonable equivalent for this small service. The facade earns its place as a reporting boundary; it does not own the monitor or repair invalid monitor state.

The records accessor returns a reference to the vector object. That avoids copying the history, but callers must respect its lifetime. Do not retain an element reference or iterator across ingest, because the commit can replace storage. A reference to the vector object itself still names records_, but its contents can change. The report uses only a short borrow and returns before any mutation. This single-threaded program does not protect a report from concurrent modification; introducing threads requires a separate synchronization design.

The report uses a classic locale and one digit after the decimal point. Locale describes formatting conventions, such as the decimal separator. Choosing it here keeps the displayed report stable across ordinary machine settings. The final output is not merely illustrative: main compares the generated string with the expected string and fails if they differ. A formatting change is therefore an intentional contract change with a visible test update.

before.title: Debug the integration by finding the earliest broken promise
paragraphs: Consider a wrong implementation that appends the converted first sample directly to records_, then rejects the second sample with an unknown unit. Before the call the history holds identifiers 1, 2, and 3. The submitted batch is {4, 21, C}, {5, 22, K}. The call throws, but the wrong history now ends at 4. A report would gain the row 4: 21.0 C ok and its record count would rise from three to four. The defect is the placement of mutation before full validation, not the wording of the exception.

Another error is rebuilding every Record::alert value after replacement. In the main scenario, reading 2 is 80 C and enters under a limit of 80. After changing the limit to 100, recomputing would print 2: 80.0 C ok and reduce the final alert count from two to one. That silently rewrites the earlier decision. The stored boolean is intentional historical data. If users want a second report that re-evaluates old samples, add it as a clearly named separate operation.

When diagnosing a failure, first write the expected state, count, last identifier, rule, and report before the action. Then trace conversion, order checks, classification, append, and commit. The first point where an invariant becomes false is more useful than the last line that crashes or prints the wrong number. A passing happy-path demonstration would miss both partial commit and rewritten history; the rejection and replacement checks exist to expose those failures.

The tests use check, which throws on a false condition. They do not use assert, whose checks can disappear in a release build when NDEBUG is defined. The rejects helper accepts a callable, runs it, and requires a logic_error-family exception. Invalid arguments and capacity errors belong to that family. Unexpected exception families still escape and fail the executable. These checks prove the listed cases, not every possible input or allocator failure.

before.title: What the compiler can prove and what execution must establish
paragraphs: The compiler verifies names, type relationships, access control, override compatibility, and the use of language syntax. It rejects an attempted copy of a unique_ptr owner. It knows that the declared rule operation is noexcept. It cannot prove that input identifiers arrive in increasing order or that a temperature is meaningful. Those depend on values that the program checks while running.

During execution, raw values enter the adapter, normalized values enter the rule, and completed records enter staged history. Control returns to ingest after each helper call. The heap-allocated concrete rule lives as long as its owning pointer keeps it. The temporary s lives for one loop iteration and is copied into a Record value before it disappears. The finished report owns its characters separately from the monitor.

For n stored records and b new samples, staging and processing take work proportional to n + b, with temporary storage proportional to n + b. A report takes work proportional to n. With the fixed capacity of eight, these costs are tightly bounded for this exercise. Removing the cap while submitting one reading at a time would repeatedly copy growing history and could cause quadratic total work. Measure against the workload before changing the design; a journal, chunked history, or a separate validated batch might support larger sessions with different tradeoffs.

The extension boundary is narrow on purpose. New unit formats belong in adaptation; new alert decisions belong behind AlertRule; new output formats belong beside the report service. A change to ordering, capacity, state rules, or transaction guarantees is a core behavior change and deserves wider tests. Patterns help only when they localize a real source of change. This capstone is complete at its stated boundary while leaving those larger system decisions visible.

Measure against the workload before changing the design; a journal, chunked history, or a separate validated batch might support larger sessions with different tradeoffs.

The extension boundary is narrow on purpose. New unit formats belong in adaptation; new alert decisions belong behind AlertRule; new output formats belong beside the report service. A change to ordering, capacity, state rules, or transaction guarantees is a core behavior change and deserves wider tests. Patterns help only when they localize a real source of change. This capstone is complete at its stated boundary while leaving those larger system decisions visible.

before.title: Code focus: The replaceable decision contract
paragraphs: The interface states the one decision that a rule must supply. It also makes deleting a derived rule through the base owning pointer safe. No specific threshold is stored in this base.
Where: Monitor stores an owning pointer to AlertRule. AtLeast derives from it, and the lab adds OutsideBand. Ingest calls this operation after conversion and ordering have succeeded.
Why: Changing the alert decision should not change unit conversion, state transitions, or commit behavior. A shared interface gives the monitor one stable call while the concrete decision varies.
Invariant: Each implementation must answer using the supplied valid sample without throwing or outside side effects. The virtual destructor must remain so ownership cleanup reaches the concrete type.
Risk: A missing override can leave a derived class abstract or select the wrong function signature. Noexcept is a promise, not a catch block; throwing from an implementation terminates the program.

before.title: Code focus: Ownership and state live in one authority
paragraphs: These private fields are the monitor's long-lived state. The owning pointer controls one rule lifetime, the vector owns stored values, and the enum names the current operating state.
Where: They are at the start of Monitor, before public operations. Constructors establish them; checked methods read or replace them. ReportFacade reaches history through a const accessor.

Why: Keeping the invariant-bearing fields private prevents callers from appending unchecked records or forcing an illegal state. One authority is easier to audit than unrelated globals or shared writable containers.

Invariant: A usable monitor has one nonnull owned rule, a valid state, and at most eight valid records in increasing order. The constructor and public methods jointly establish and preserve this contract.

Risk: A raw borrowed rule pointer could outlive its rule. Exposing a mutable records vector would let callers bypass capacity and conversion checks. Raising capacity affects the cost of each staged copy.

before.title: Code focus: Guard a transition before changing state
paragraphs: Start has one legal source state. The check rejects any other source before the state field changes, so a failed request leaves the machine where it was.
Where: This is a public Monitor member. Main calls it after construction, and run_checks also calls it from illegal states to verify rejection.
Why: A named operation keeps state rules beside the mutation they protect. Callers request an action rather than manufacturing a new enum value themselves.
Invariant: Only an idle monitor may enter running through start. A stopped object cannot restart, and a running object cannot be started twice.
Risk: Assigning running before checking idle destroys the evidence needed by the guard. Removing the guard would allow a stopped session to restart while retaining old history.

before.title: Code focus: Prepare a candidate without altering accepted history
paragraphs: A copy becomes the candidate history. Each new sample is normalized and checked against the most recent candidate record, so the same ordering rule covers both old and new items.
Where: This block follows state and capacity validation in ingest. Classification and staged append follow it; the final swap is outside the loop.
Why: Checking only records_.back() would miss a duplicate within the new batch. Checking staged.back() sees the accepted past plus every earlier proposed item without committing any of them.

Invariant: Before each iteration, staged contains valid increasing records. Before the final swap, records_ still holds exactly the original history, even if conversion or ordering rejects a later item.
Risk: Replacing staged with a reference to records_ would destroy isolation. Reading staged.back() without first testing empty would be invalid for the first reading in an empty session.

before.title: Code focus: Store the intake decision, then commit once
paragraphs: The chosen rule produces a boolean, a proposed record stores it, and one vector swap makes the completed batch visible. The flag becomes historical data at this point.
Where: This block is the end of ingest. The loop repeats classification and append for each valid sample; swap runs once after the loop ends successfully.

Why: Keeping the commit outside the loop gives a late rejection the same effect as an early rejection: no accepted history change. Storing the boolean prevents a later rule replacement from rewriting the past.
Invariant: Every staged record has been normalized, ordered, and classified. The live vector changes exactly once on success and never changes on an ordinary pre-commit exception.

Risk: Moving swap into the loop produces partial commits. Re-evaluating flags during reporting changes the meaning of history. Side effects inside alert would lie outside the vector rollback guarantee.

paragraphs: The loop formats accepted values and counts their stored flags. It does not ask the current rule to judge old readings, and it does not change monitor state.

Invariant: Each row reflects a stored normalized sample and its original alert flag. Output order matches history order, and the resulting string owns its characters independently of the monitor.
Risk: Retaining an element reference for later use can become unsafe after ingest replaces vector storage. A report must not run concurrently with mutation without a synchronization contract.
